# Function methods and implementation notes {#sec-methods}

These entries follow the archived 2.0.9004 implementation. Each gives the documented calculation, its implementation file, a direct link to the complete help topic and links back to the chapters that use it. Detailed scientific comparisons are developed in the linked methods chapters. An entry derived from the package documentation is not a new validation result. [Download the exact package source, including NEWS and Rd references](archives/skyscapeR_2.0.9004.tar.gz).

## Time, coordinates and ephemerides {#group-time}

State the time scale, civil calendar, reference frame and refraction convention before comparing outputs. A correct calendar conversion can still pass the wrong physical instant to a downstream calculation.

### `astroYear()` {#fn-astroyear}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-astroyear)

```{=html}
<p>Astronomical years include zero. Historical BC or BCE years convert
by subtracting the historical year from one. AD and CE years keep their value.
Era labels are case-insensitive and follow a positive whole year.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** When an excavation report gives 1 BC, the corresponding astronomical year is zero. Convert the year once before computing an ephemeris. An off-by-one year can survive a round trip through calendar formatting if both ends use the same mistaken convention.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>x</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Numeric astronomical years, character integer years, or historical labels.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Numeric astronomical years in input order.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/dates.R`. [Full function help](help/astroYear.html) · [Time, coordinates and ephemerides outline](contents-plan.html#plan-time) · [Astronomical conventions and stellar positions](astronomical-conventions.html#conventions-time)

### `BC.AD()` {#fn-bc-ad}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-bc-ad)

```{=html}
<p>Astronomical dating includes a year zero, whereas historical BC and AD labels run
directly from 1 BC to AD 1. Positive years retain their number and receive AD. For zero
or a negative year, subtract the astronomical year from one and append BC. The
conversion works element by element and changes only the label, not the calendar or
instant.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** When an excavation report gives 1 BC, the corresponding astronomical year is zero. Convert the year once before computing an ephemeris. An off-by-one year can survive a round trip through calendar formatting if both ends use the same mistaken convention.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Numeric astronomical year or vector of years. Year zero is 1 BC. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Character labels for astronomical years. Year 0 is 1 BC and year -1 is 2 BC.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/dates.R`. [Full function help](help/BC.AD.html) · [Time, coordinates and ephemerides outline](contents-plan.html#plan-time) · [Astronomical conventions and stellar positions](astronomical-conventions.html#conventions-time)

### `body.position()` {#fn-body-position}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-body-position)

```{=html}
<p>An alignment comparison needs an epoch, a reference frame and, for a local sightline, a
site. Character times are converted to UT Julian dates using the selected calendar and
timezone; numeric times are already UT Julian dates. Swiss Ephemeris supplies right
ascension and declination. Without a site the function uses the geocentric frame. With a
site it can use a topocentric position and convert to local azimuth and altitude. A
vector of times is evaluated one instant at a time and returned in input order.
</p>
<p>Only the horizon object's location is used; its altitude profile is not used
to determine whether the body is visible above the terrain. With a location,
horizontal altitude is apparent when refraction is TRUE and geometric when
FALSE. Azimuth is measured clockwise from north.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Astrodienst. Swiss Ephemeris programmer's manual. <a href="https://www.astro.com/swisseph/swephprg.htm">https://www.astro.com/swisseph/swephprg.htm</a>.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Use the same instant, coordinate frame, observer, refraction and ephemeris files when comparing against another engine. Agreement in equatorial coordinates alone leaves the local horizontal conversion untested.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>time</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Either a string containing the date and time in the format "YYYY/MM/DD HH:MM:SS"
(see <code>timestring</code>), or a numeric containing the julian date (see <code>time2jd</code>).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>obj</code></th><td><code>&quot;sun&quot;</code></td><td><p>String containing name of the solar system body of interest. Can be
any of the planets (inc. Pluto), the Moon, the Sun or the Ecliptic. Defaults to 'sun'.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Observer location: a numeric vector containing latitude and
longitude in degrees and elevation in metres, in that order, or a
<em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object whose metadata supplies those coordinates.
Required for topocentric coordinates and for horizontal output in either
frame. With no location, only geocentric equatorial coordinates are returned.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Timezone for civil timestamps. Use UTC or a fixed offset for dates before 1900. See <code>time2jd</code> for named zones and offsets.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Calendar for civil dates. Use <code>"G"</code> for Gregorian or <code>"J"</code> for Julian.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>dec</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Output declination: <em>geo</em> for the geocentric, or <em>topo</em> for the topocentric
frame of reference. If not given the value set by <code>skyscapeR.vars</code> will be used instead.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Logical. Apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Atmospheric pressure in mbar. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>T</code></td><td><p>Logical. Display progress or informational messages. Default <code>TRUE</code>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A list containing an <code>equatorial</code> data frame with columns
<code>RA</code> and <code>Dec</code>, in degrees. When <code>loc</code> is supplied, the list
also contains a <code>horizontal</code> data frame with columns <code>az</code> and
<code>alt</code>, in degrees. Each data frame has one row per input time.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/mechanics.R`. ### `jd2time()` {#fn-jd2time}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-jd2time)

```{=html}
<p>An instant is specified by its UT Julian date. To label it consistently, choose the
calendar and the offset or civil timezone appropriate to the record. The conversion
rounds to the nearest second, applies the offset at the rounded instant, handles day
rollover and converts the day number with Swiss Ephemeris.
</p>
<p>Fixed offsets may be numeric hours east of UTC (for example 5.5), or
strings such as <code>"UTC+05:30"</code>, <code>"UTC-02"</code> or <code>"GMT+01"</code>.
Offsets must lie between -14 and +14 hours. UTC, GMT and the empty string
mean zero offset; an empty string does not select the system timezone.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** For an ancient event near local midnight, retain the UT Julian day alongside the printed date. Round-tripping a civil label tests conversion conventions; it cannot establish the prehistoric difference between terrestrial and rotational time.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>jd</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Finite numeric vector of UT Julian dates.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Timezone name or fixed offset; defaults to the value in <code>skyscapeR.vars()</code>. See Details.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Output calendar: G or Gregorian, J or Julian. Defaults to the package calendar setting, initially Gregorian.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>F</code></td><td><p>Logical; display a conversion message. Default is FALSE.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A character vector in YYYY/MM/DD HH:MM:SS format. Years are signed as needed and are not padded to four digits.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/dates.R`. ### `long.date()` {#fn-long-date}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-long-date)

```{=html}
<p>A season or event table may need a day/month label without an epoch. The first two
characters are the month number and characters four and five the day number; the
separator occupies position three. The month is looked up in R's English month
abbreviations. This formatting step does not validate a calendar date or convert between
calendars.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** These are representation changes. Preserve the original field string so the conversion can be inspected, especially for negative angles smaller than one degree or a date recorded without its clock or timezone.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>date</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>date in 'MM-DD' format</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Character month-and-day labels such as "21 Jun", derived from the supplied month and day.
</p>
```

</details>

### `obliquity()` {#fn-obliquity}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-obliquity)

```{=html}
<p>The tilt changes over archaeological timescales. For each supplied astronomical year the
calculation uses Gregorian 1 January at noon UT, requests the obliquity/nutation record
from Swiss Ephemeris and returns its first element, the true obliquity in degrees. An
annual value is a reference for limiting declinations rather than a search for the
instant of solstice.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Laskar, J. et al. (2004), A long-term numerical
solution for the insolation quantities of the Earth, <em>Astron.
Astroph.</em>, 428, 261-285, doi:10.1051/0004-6361:20041335.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Separate the annual obliquity reference from the approximate local parallax correction. A limiting declination used as a target has a different meaning from a position calculated for an observed instant.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$cur.year</code></td><td><p>Year for which to calculate the obliquity. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.
Defaults to present year as given by <em>Sys.Date</em></p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Numeric obliquity of the ecliptic in degrees, one value per astronomical year.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/mechanics.R`. ### `parallax.corr()` {#fn-parallax-corr}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-parallax-corr)

```{=html}
<p>The limiting-declination functions subtract this approximate correction from their
geocentric target. The correction in degrees is the supplied parallax multiplied by the
cosine of altitude and sine of latitude, with the angular arguments evaluated in
degrees. The sign therefore reverses between hemispheres. This scalar approximation is
distinct from computing an instantaneous topocentric ephemeris.
</p>
<p>Ruggles gives an archaeological example of applying mean lunar parallax in a
declination calculator.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Ruggles, C. L. N. Basic declination calculator. <a href="https://web.cliveruggles.com/tools/declination-calculator">https://web.cliveruggles.com/tools/declination-calculator</a>.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Separate the annual obliquity reference from the approximate local parallax correction. A limiting declination used as a target has a different meaning from a position calculated for an observed instant.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>parallax</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Average parallax to correct (e.g. 0.00224 for the Sun, or 0.952 for the Moon)</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>This can be either the latitude of the location, or a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>altitude</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Altitude of the celestial object. Defaults to 0 degrees.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Numeric declination correction in degrees. The sign depends on latitude.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/mechanics.R`. ### `skyscapeR.vars()` {#fn-skyscaper-vars}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-skyscaper-vars)

```{=html}
<p>The same observation can have different labels or apparent coordinates under different
calendar, timezone, reference-frame or atmospheric choices. With no arguments the
function returns a named snapshot. Supplied arguments update the package environment for
subsequent calls in the current R session. Functions with their own explicit arguments
or fixed UT sampling conventions may override these defaults. Record the settings with
the survey data.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Schaefer, B. E. (1986). Atmospheric Extinction Effects on Stellar Alignments. Journal for the History of Astronomy 17, S32-S42. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182868601701003")}.
</p>
<p>Schaefer, B. E. (1993). Astronomy and the Limits of Vision. Vistas in Astronomy 36, 311-361. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/0083-6656(93)90113-X")}.
</p>
<p>University of California, Davis. <em>Physics 157 Observing Guide</em>, Spring 2022, discussion of extinction coefficients.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Save the resolved settings at the time of computation. Reproducing the written R call under another session's refraction, pressure or calendar defaults can produce a different result.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Timezone name (for example "Europe/London") or fixed offset in hours east of UTC,
or a string such as "UTC+02:00". Initially "Europe/London". Use UTC or a fixed
offset for dates before 1900. See <code>time2jd</code> for details.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Calendar for civil dates. Use <code>"G"</code> for Gregorian or <code>"J"</code> for Julian.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Whether atmospheric refraction is to be taken into account. Default is TRUE.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Air pressure in mbar for the refraction calculation. Default is 1013.25 mbar.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius for the refraction calculation. Default is 15 degrees Celsius.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>dec</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Output declination: <em>geo</em> for the geocentric, or <em>topo</em> for the topocentric
frame of reference. Defaults to topocentric.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>k</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Visual extinction in magnitudes per airmass, shared by natural sky sketches and stellar phase calculations. The initial value of 0.2 is a clear-sky baseline, consistent with the approximate V-band coefficient for Kitt Peak in the UC Davis Physics 157 Observing Guide. Extinction varies with site and atmospheric conditions (Schaefer 1986, 1993). Use zero to disable extinction.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A named list of the current session settings, including the current year. Supplying an argument updates that setting for subsequent package calls in this R session.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/global_vars.R`. ### `ten()` {#fn-ten}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-ten)

```{=html}
<p>The sign applies to the whole angle. The magnitude is the sum of absolute degrees,
minutes divided by 60 and seconds divided by 3600. With numeric components the first
nonzero component sets the sign and later components must be nonnegative. A string may
contain one to three colon- or space-separated components and an optional leading sign.
A string such as "-0:30" preserves the negative sign even when degrees are zero.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** These are representation changes. Preserve the original field string so the conversion can be inspected, especially for negative angles smaller than one degree or a date recorded without its clock or timezone.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>dd</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Degrees as a finite numeric scalar, or a single character string
containing an angle, for example <code>"-8:30:00"</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>mm</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Arcminutes as a finite numeric scalar. Defaults to zero.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>ss</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Arcseconds as a finite numeric scalar. Defaults to zero.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A numeric scalar giving the angle in signed decimal degrees.
</p>
```

</details>

### `time2jd()` {#fn-time2jd}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-time2jd)

```{=html}
<p>Civil dates require both a calendar and a time convention to specify an instant. The
function parses each supplied date and time, verifies that the calendar date exists by
converting it to a Julian date and back, then applies the chosen offset or civil
timezone to obtain UT. A date without a time uses local midnight. Astronomical year
numbering includes year zero. An era label can also precede the month, for example
<code>"3700 BCE/06/21"</code>.
</p>
<p>Fixed offsets may be numeric hours east of UTC (for example 5.5), or
strings such as <code>"UTC+05:30"</code>, <code>"UTC-02"</code> or <code>"GMT+01"</code>.
Offsets must lie between -14 and +14 hours. UTC, GMT and the empty string
mean zero offset; an empty string does not select the system timezone.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** For an ancient event near local midnight, retain the UT Julian day alongside the printed date. Round-tripping a civil label tests conversion conventions; it cannot establish the prehistoric difference between terrestrial and rotational time.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>time</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Character vector in YYYY/MM/DD format, optionally followed by HH:MM or HH:MM:SS. Fractional seconds are accepted. Omitted clock time means midnight.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Timezone name or fixed offset; defaults to the value in <code>skyscapeR.vars()</code>. See Details.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Calendar: G or Gregorian, J or Julian. Defaults to the package calendar setting, initially Gregorian.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>F</code></td><td><p>Logical; display a conversion message. Default is FALSE.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A numeric vector of UT Julian dates, in the same order as time.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/dates.R`. ### `timestring()` {#fn-timestring}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-timestring)

```{=html}
<p>Survey records often store year, month, day and clock time separately. This formatter
pads the month, day and clock components to two characters and joins them as
year/month/day and hours:minutes:seconds. Omitted time is noon. Formatting alone does
not supply a timezone or check that the date exists; use time2jd to validate and convert
it.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** These are representation changes. Preserve the original field string so the conversion can be inspected, especially for negative angles smaller than one degree or a date recorded without its clock or timezone.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Year. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>month</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Month</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>day</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Day</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>hour</code></th><td><code>12</code></td><td><p>Hour</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>minute</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Minute</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>second</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Second</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A character date-time string in the slash-separated format accepted by <code>time2jd</code>.
</p>
```

## Reducing field observations {#group-survey}

The reduced true bearing depends on which direction or solar limb was observed, when it was observed and whether a magnetic correction was supplied. A field reduction and a test of the subsequent skyline have different reference data.

### `mag.dec()` {#fn-mag-dec}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-mag-dec)

```{=html}
<p>Compass reduction depends on when and where the reading was taken. The function
evaluates IGRF-14 through oce at sea level and returns east-positive declination.
Supply a single site for several dates, a single date for several sites, or
one date per site. Results follow input order. Other size combinations raise
an error. The calendar date is converted to a decimal year using the actual
length of that year at midnight UTC. Supported dates run from 1 January 1900
through 1 January 2030 inclusive. Site elevation is ignored by this model call.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Kelley, D. and Richards, C. oce: magneticField. <a href="https://dankelley.github.io/oce/reference/magneticField.html">https://dankelley.github.io/oce/reference/magneticField.html</a>.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** An externally supplied magnetic correction and a modelled IGRF value are alternative inputs. Keep the correction's sign, survey date and origin with the field data. Agreement with a regional magnetic model does not rule out local disturbance at the instrument.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Latitude and longitude in degrees as a vector, matrix or data frame with one row per site, or a horizon object. An optional third column gives elevation.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>date</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>One or more survey dates as Date objects or YYYY/MM/DD strings.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Numeric magnetic declination in degrees. Use it as the correction added to a magnetic bearing in <code>reduct.compass</code>.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/misc.R`. [Full function help](help/mag.dec.html) · [Reducing field observations outline](contents-plan.html#plan-survey) · [Reducing field observations](field-reduction.html#field-compass) · [Reduce compass readings to true azimuth](vignette-guide.html#workflow-reduce-compass-readings-to-true-azimuth)

### `reduct.compass()` {#fn-reduct-compass}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-reduct-compass)

```{=html}
<p>Magnetic north differs from true north at the time and place of survey. Add the supplied
magnetic declination to each magnetic bearing, or calculate it from the survey
coordinates and date with mag.dec. Corrected bearings are rounded using the input
bearing representation. With an explicit altitude or a measured horizon, the corrected
bearing also enters the conversion to declination.
</p>
<p>Supply either a measurement date or a known magnetic declination.
If both are given, the supplied magnetic declination is used and the date is
retained in the output. Explicit altitude values take precedence over a
horizon profile. Otherwise, each measurement's corrected true azimuth is
used to retrieve its horizon altitude; the same altitude is reported and
used to calculate celestial declination. Supply one site and date for the whole
survey or one location row and/or date per bearing, in measurement order.
A supplied correction can likewise be shared or paired with each bearing.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** An externally supplied magnetic correction and a modelled IGRF value are alternative inputs. Keep the correction's sign, survey date and origin with the field data. Agreement with a regional magnetic model does not rule out local disturbance at the instrument.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Location, either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> or a vector
containing the latitude, longitude and elevation of location, in this order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>mag.az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Array of magnetic azimuth measurements.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>date</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Date of measurements as a string in the format: 'YYYY/MM/DD'.
Only necessary if <em>magdec</em> is not given. When omitted, the output
Date column contains missing values (NA).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>magdec</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Magnetic declination, if known.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Altitude, necessary for automatic declination calculation.
If missing and <em>loc</em> is a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object then the altitude
will be automatically read from the horizon profile.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Names or labels to identify each measurement.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>ID</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>IDs or codes to identify each measurement.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>HWT.ID</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>HeyWhatsThat IDs relating to a previously generated
horizon profile for measurement.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A data frame with one row per measurement, including location,
magnetic azimuth, date, magnetic declination and true azimuth. Altitude and
celestial declination are included when altitudes are supplied or a horizon
is available. Optional identification columns are retained.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/data-reduction.R`. ### `reduct.theodolite()` {#fn-reduct-theodolite}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-reduct-theodolite)

```{=html}
<p>The observed difference between the instrument readings to the structure and to the Sun
is added to the calculated solar azimuth at the observation time. The routine handles a
circle-boundary difference, accounts for the selected solar limb through sunAz and
rounds the reference bearing according to the input readings. An explicit altitude or a
supplied horizon allows the corrected bearing to be converted to declination. Correct
time, civil timezone, limb and site are all essential to the reduction.
</p>
<p>Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing <span class="pkg">swephRdata</span>; see <code>skyscapeR-package</code> for setup.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Ruggles, C.L.N. (1999). <em>Astronomy in Prehistoric Britain and Ireland</em>.
Yale University Press.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** For a solar sight, the measured limb, civil time, timezone and instrument readings define a single observation. The useful independent check is recovery of a known terrestrial bearing from that observation.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Location, either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> or a vector
containing the latitude, longitude and elevation of location, in this order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Array of azimuths. Use <code>ten</code> to convert to
decimal degrees if necessary.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>date</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Date of measurements as a string in the format: 'YYYY/MM/DD'</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>time</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Time of sun-sight measurement in the format: 'HH:MM:SS'</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>tz</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Timezone of input either as a known acronym (e.g. "GMT", "CET") or
a string with continent followed by country capital (e.g. "Europe/London").</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>az.sun</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Measured azimuth of the sun. Defaults to zero.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>limb</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Measured limb of the sun. Options are <em>left</em>, <em>right</em>.
If missing the center of the sun will be used for calculations.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Altitude, necessary for automatic declination calculation.
If missing and <em>loc</em> is a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object then the altitude
will be automatically read from the horizon profile.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Names or labels to identify each measurement.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>ID</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>IDs or codes to identify each measurement.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>HWT.ID</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>HeyWhatsThat IDs relating to a previously generated
horizon profile for measurement.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A data frame with one row per observation. True.Azimuth is the corrected azimuth in degrees. The table also records the observed azimuth, solar azimuth, time and site coordinates. Where available it includes Altitude and Declination in degrees and the supplied identifiers.
</p>
```

</details>

### `sunAz()` {#fn-sunaz}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-sunaz)

```{=html}
<p>A solar reference requires the observer position, timestamp, timezone and the part of
the disc that was sighted. Times are parsed using R's civil-time routines and converted
to UT Julian dates. Swiss Ephemeris supplies the topocentric solar position and its
horizontal coordinates using 1013.25 mbar and 15 degrees Celsius. The returned bearing
is measured clockwise from north. Sighting the left or right limb applies a fixed minus
or plus 16 arcminutes in azimuth. Optional altitude is the geometric centre altitude.
</p>
<p>Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing <span class="pkg">swephRdata</span>; see <code>skyscapeR-package</code> for setup.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** For a solar sight, the measured limb, civil time, timezone and instrument readings define a single observation. The useful independent check is recovery of a known terrestrial bearing from that observation.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Location, either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> or a vector
containing the latitude, longitude and elevation of location, in this order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>time</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>String containing the date and time in the following format:
"YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Timezone for civil timestamps. Use UTC or a fixed offset for dates before 1900. See <code>time2jd</code> for named zones and offsets.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>limb</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Measured limb of the sun. Options are <em>left</em>, <em>right</em>.
If missing the center of the sun will be output.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>Logical that triggers output of altitude of the sun at exact time.
Default is FALSE.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Solar azimuth in degrees clockwise from north, one value per observation. With alt = TRUE, a data frame with columns az and alt is returned. The altitude is geometric and is expressed in degrees.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/mechanics.R`. ## Terrain horizons and panoramas {#group-terrain}

Coordinate reference systems, viewpoint, vertical datum and missing terrain affect the computed skyline. Photographic calibration introduces a separate angular reference. Export, colour and image relinking have different effects from changing the numerical horizon.

### `createHor()` {#fn-createhor}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-createhor) · [H01 field validation](study-register.qmd#h01-field-validation)

```{=html}
<p><strong>Measured bearings.</strong> To evaluate sightlines between measured bearings, the constructor repeats the azimuths
one turn in each direction, removes duplicate azimuth entries and linearly interpolates
altitude and altitude uncertainty onto a 0.01-degree grid from -90 to 450 degrees.
Scalar uncertainty is repeated. Optional smoothing applies a running mean over the
specified number of grid samples to both series, with zero fill at the outer ends.
Latitude, longitude and elevation identify the observer; omitted elevation defaults to
zero. Interpolation cannot recover narrow features between measurements.
</p>
<p><strong>Observer and DEM coverage.</strong> For a DEM, supply a point with a CRS, projected x and y with loc.crs, or WGS84 latitude and longitude.
The optional third coordinate is ground elevation in metres in the DEM's vertical
datum. Otherwise ground elevation is bilinearly sampled at the site. Observer
elevation in the returned georeference is ground elevation plus eye.height.
A terrain model represents bare earth. A surface model includes the objects
represented in its elevations. Use a single continuous band in metres with a
defined horizontal CRS. Missing samples and terrain beyond the raster edge are skipped. A warning and the incomplete.bearings metadata identify incomplete coverage. Each bearing needs at least one usable sample.
</p>
```

**Accuracy, uncertainty and reproducibility.**

```{=html}
<p>H01 compared 334 bearings at 31 observing setups.
At the surveyed bearings, <code>createHor()</code> reproduced the observed terrain skyline to within half a degree in 91.9% of cases.
</p>
<p>The numerical skyline is a maximum over sampled terrain, not an accuracy
certificate for the DEM. Horizontal and vertical datum differences, observer
height, missing raster values, vegetation and buildings can exceed the sampling
error. DEM elevations and a supplied observer ground elevation must use a
compatible vertical datum. No geoid conversion or vertical-datum correction is
performed automatically. Refine the angular and distance sampling and expand
the radius until the relevant sightlines are stable. Compare with surveyed
bearings and altitudes where available.
</p>
<p><code>alt.unc</code> is supplied by the user and is not estimated from DEM resolution,
control residuals or atmospheric variability. Smoothing a measured profile can
remove narrow notches or peaks. Adaptive panorama sampling and illustrative
lighting concern the image; they do not increase numerical horizon precision.
The terrestrial refraction approximation assumes the supplied atmosphere and
cannot reproduce all near-ground gradients or mirage conditions.
</p>
<p>Save the DEM provenance, observer location and datum, constructor arguments,
feature objects, returned horizon and external PNG. Rebuilding from the same
source is distinct from merely replotting the saved horizon.
</p>



```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Patat, F. (2011). Horizon synthesis for archaeo-astronomical purposes. Astronomische Nachrichten 332, 743-749. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1002/asna.201111570")}.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A feature height is additional relief on the supplied surface. A bank can be visible below the terrain skyline, so inspect the numerical profile and panorama separately. The [H01](study-register.qmd#h01-field-validation) field residuals quantify agreement at surveyed terrain bearings. Reconstructed features need their own reference measurements.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Array of azimuth values</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Array of altitude values.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Observer location. For DEMs, pass a single CRS-bearing terra SpatVector point directly as loc, or a numeric latitude and longitude. Ground elevation is read from the DEM unless supplied as a third numeric value. Measured horizons take latitude, longitude and elevation.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>dem</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional single-band terra SpatRaster or local raster filename.
Supply dem in place of az and alt. Requires the optional terra package.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc.crs</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>CRS for numeric DEM observer coordinates in x,y order (easting, northing or longitude, latitude). Without it, numeric loc uses latitude, longitude in WGS84. A single terra SpatVector point carries its own CRS. An optional third numeric coordinate is ground elevation in metres.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td><code>&quot;&quot;</code></td><td><p>Name of site.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt.unc</code></th><td><code>0.5</code></td><td><p>Either a single value or an array of altitude
uncertainty.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>smooth</code></th><td><code>F</code></td><td><p>Logical to control whether to smooth horizon profile using rolling mean.
Defaults to FALSE</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.scale</code></th><td><code>1000</code></td><td><p>Number of samples in the rolling mean when smooth = TRUE. The grid spacing is 0.01 degrees, so 1000 samples span approximately 10 degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>eye.height</code></th><td><code>1.6</code></td><td><p>Observer height above the selected ground elevation in metres.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>max.distance</code></th><td><code>10000</code></td><td><p>DEM search radius in metres, default 10000. Include any
distant terrain that could form the horizon within the DEM coverage.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>az.step</code></th><td><code>0.25</code></td><td><p>Maximum spacing of numerical DEM rays in degrees. The default
is 0.25. An equal number of steps fills the circle.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>distance.step</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Maximum spacing of samples along each ray in metres.
By default use half the smaller native cell dimension estimated at the site.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>features</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional <code>horFeature</code> object or list of such
objects describing reconstructed or highlighted structures. Requires dem.
Elevations are additive, with the largest positive and deepest negative
contributions combined at overlaps. Later footprints take colour precedence.
Features affect both numerical horizon and visible terrain. Their geometry
is kept out of the returned horizon; save the feature objects separately.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>curvature</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Apply Earth curvature to DEM sightlines. Default TRUE.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction.k</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Default NULL applies Patat when curvature is enabled. Set zero for geometric curvature without terrestrial refraction, or supply a coefficient below one for the effective-radius model.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$atm</code></td><td><p>Ground atmospheric pressure in millibars for Patat terrestrial refraction.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$temp</code></td><td><p>Ground air temperature in degrees Celsius.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>tempgrad</code></th><td><code>-10</code></td><td><p>Vertical temperature gradient in kelvins per kilometre (default -10).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>panorama</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Render an external terrain PNG for a DEM. Default TRUE.
Set FALSE for the numerical horizon alone.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>width</code></th><td><code>4096</code></td><td><p>DEM panorama width in pixels, an even integer from 32 to 81920.
Default 4096 by 2048 pixels. Height is half the width. Widths above 8192 are assembled from temporary image tiles. Both dimensions grow with width, so a tenfold increase generates 100 times as many pixels.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>panorama.distance.step</code></th><td><code>&quot;adaptive&quot;</code></td><td><p>The default, "adaptive", starts at one local DEM cell and increases radial
spacing with distance using the larger of the requested angular acuity and
one horizontal PNG pixel. This transverse footprint is a proxy for radial
detail. A narrow ridge may fall between samples. Use a positive number for
fixed spacing in metres or NULL to reuse distance.step. The numerical horizon
uses distance.step independently. Inspect metadata$image$sampling for the
effective angle, sample count and actual step range. On large DEM-only panoramas, the renderer checks near terrain against a conservative upper bound for the remaining terrain on each ray. It skips distant samples only where all remaining elevations are hidden and keeps neighbours for surface shading. Terrain with added archaeological features uses the full sampling path.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>panorama.acuity</code></th><td><code>1</code></td><td><p>Angular detail target in arcminutes for adaptive PNG sampling. Defaults to 1 (nominal 20/20 acuity). Larger values coarsen distant terrain.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>terrain.palette</code></th><td><code>&quot;temperate&quot;</code></td><td><p>Named land/water pair from <code>demPalettes</code>.
Options are temperate (default), standalone, arid, alpine, coastal and relief.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>land_cols</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Opaque R colour names or hex colours in increasing
elevation order. NULL inherits the respective ramp from terrain.palette.
Supply either vector to override just that ramp. One colour gives a uniform base. Colours interpolate in Lab space.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>sea_cols</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Opaque R colour names or hex colours in increasing
elevation order. NULL inherits the respective ramp from terrain.palette.
Supply either vector to override just that ramp. One colour gives a uniform base. Colours interpolate in Lab space.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>sea_level</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>DEM elevation in metres at or below which the sea colour
ramp is used. Default 0. A level water surface uses the shallow colour. This is an elevation threshold. Use NULL to apply
the land palette over the whole visible elevation range, including depressions.
The temperate land ramp starts at the lowest visible land level or sea threshold, whichever is higher. Other palettes with a threshold start at sea_level. The ramp ends at the highest
visible elevation. The sea ramp starts at the lowest visible elevation.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>n_sea</code></th><td><code>3L</code></td><td><p>Number of entries reserved for the sea ramp, leaving at least
two land colours. Default 3.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>palette_n</code></th><td><code>256L</code></td><td><p>Total number of palette entries, from 4 to 65536. Default
256.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>lighting</code></th><td><code>c(&quot;relief&quot;, &quot;directional&quot;)</code></td><td><p>Relief lighting (default) blends a light at the observer (75 percent)
with the directional source (25 percent). It shades both sides of a slope and
lifts deep shadows. Choose "directional"
for one-sided hillshade. Lighting affects the PNG only.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>light.azimuth</code></th><td><code>315</code></td><td><p>Direction towards the illustrative light
source in degrees clockwise from true north and above the horizon. Defaults
are 315 and 45 degrees. Hillshading uses upward surface normals in metric
east, north and vertical coordinates. This is local illumination without
cast shadows from other terrain.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>light.altitude</code></th><td><code>45</code></td><td><p>Direction towards the illustrative light
source in degrees clockwise from true north and above the horizon. Defaults
are 315 and 45 degrees. Hillshading uses upward surface normals in metric
east, north and vertical coordinates. This is local illumination without
cast shadows from other terrain.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>ambient</code></th><td><code>0.38</code></td><td><p>Fraction of illumination retained on slopes facing away from
the light (0 to 1). Default 0.38. Use 1 for unshaded palette colours.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>haze</code></th><td><code>0.65</code></td><td><p>Maximum fraction of distance haze (0 to 1). Default 0.65.
Set haze=0 and ambient=1 to inspect the colour mapping alone.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>image.dir</code></th><td><code>getwd()</code></td><td><p>Directory for the DEM PNG. Defaults to the working directory. Site names form the filename; different images with the same name receive a checksum suffix.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>attribution</code></th><td><code>&quot;User-supplied DEM&quot;</code></td><td><p>Credit for the DEM, included in plots and exports. The generic default credit is omitted from plots.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>license</code></th><td><code>&quot;See source DEM terms&quot;</code></td><td><p>Source licence or terms for the DEM, included in exports.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>ncores</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Maximum DEM tracing workers. Defaults to half the available logical cores, rounded down with a minimum of one. The startup message reports used and available cores. Workers share file-backed DEM data and process separate bearings.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Announce the DEM radius, sampling and rendering stages.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>progress</code></th><td><code>interactive() &amp;&amp; verbose</code></td><td><p>Show a progress bar for each tracing stage. Default on in interactive verbose sessions.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.horizon list with metadata (site name and georeference) and a data frame named data. Its az, alt and alt.unc columns contain azimuth, horizon altitude and altitude uncertainty, all in degrees.
</p><h5>Accuracy, uncertainty and reproducibility</h5><p>H01 compared 334 bearings at 31 observing setups.
At the surveyed bearings, <code>createHor()</code> reproduced the observed terrain skyline to within half a degree in 91.9% of cases.
</p>
<p>The numerical skyline is a maximum over sampled terrain, not an accuracy
certificate for the DEM. Horizontal and vertical datum differences, observer
height, missing raster values, vegetation and buildings can exceed the sampling
error. DEM elevations and a supplied observer ground elevation must use a
compatible vertical datum. No geoid conversion or vertical-datum correction is
performed automatically. Refine the angular and distance sampling and expand
the radius until the relevant sightlines are stable. Compare with surveyed
bearings and altitudes where available.
</p><p><code>alt.unc</code> is supplied by the user and is not estimated from DEM resolution,
control residuals or atmospheric variability. Smoothing a measured profile can
remove narrow notches or peaks. Adaptive panorama sampling and illustrative
lighting concern the image; they do not increase numerical horizon precision.
The terrestrial refraction approximation assumes the supplied atmosphere and
cannot reproduce all near-ground gradients or mirage conditions.
</p><p>Save the DEM provenance, observer location and datum, constructor arguments,
feature objects, returned horizon and external PNG. Rebuilding from the same
source is distinct from merely replotting the saved horizon.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/horizon.R`. ### `createHWT()` {#fn-createhwt}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-createhwt)

```{=html}
<p>A digital horizon supplies estimated angular obstruction around the site. The
optional httr2 package submits one HTTPS request for a panorama. Once the
service returns its identifier, the function waits two minutes before the first readiness check, then polls at intervals
of up to 15 seconds. The polling deadline defaults to 600 seconds. If the wait
expires, use the identifier with downloadHWT once the panorama is ready.
Individual requests have a timeout of at most 30 seconds. The initial submission
and final download are separate from the polling time allowance. Once ready,
the profile is downloaded and assigned the supplied name. Terrain-derived
profiles need field verification where vegetation or structures affect visibility.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p><a href="https://www.heywhatsthat.com/">HeyWhatsThat.com</a>
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Separate where a provider actually placed its viewpoint from the coordinate in the request. Record the downloaded profile, reference direction and acquisition date. A provider comparison can mix terrain-source and algorithm differences.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>lat</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>The latitude of the location.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>lon</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>The longitude of the location.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Name assigned to the returned horizon profile.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>elevation</code></th><td><code>1.6</code></td><td><p>The elevation of the observer above
ground level in meters. Default is 1.6 meters (eye level).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>src</code></th><td><code>&quot;skyscapeR&quot;</code></td><td><p>Request source ID for <em>HeyWhatsThat</em>. Default is
'skyscapeR'. Only change this if you have been given a source ID by the
creator of <em>HeyWhatsThat</em>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>max.wait</code></th><td><code>600</code></td><td><p>Maximum seconds to wait for panorama readiness after submission. Default 600.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Logical switch to control output. Default is <em>TRUE</em>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.horizon object for the requested panorama, as returned by <code>downloadHWT</code>. This function submits a remote request and waits for the calculated profile.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/horizon.R`. [Full function help](help/createHWT.html) · [Terrain horizons and panoramas outline](contents-plan.html#plan-terrain) · [Importing site horizons](vignette-guide.html#workflow-importing-site-horizons)

### `demPalettes()` {#fn-dempalettes}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-dempalettes)

```{=html}
<p>Pass a preset name to the terrain.palette argument of <code>createHor</code>.
Use <code>demPalettes("standalone")</code> to inspect the colours in that preset.
Temperate uses green and ochre, arid uses sand and red-brown, alpine runs
from forest greens to pale rock and white, and coastal pairs sand and grass
with a deep-blue to turquoise water ramp. Relief gives land one neutral tint
for inspecting slope shading. Each preset has its own sea_cols vector.
Land stops are ordered low to high and water stops deep to shallow.
<code>createHor</code> treats elevations at or below sea_level as water for colouring.
An inland depression below that threshold also receives the water tint.
sea_level=NULL uses the land ramp for all elevations.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Terrain colour, shading and cropping can make a landform easier to recognise. Evaluate the profile at the archaeological bearing for a numerical claim about horizon altitude.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional exact preset name. Omit to retrieve the full catalogue.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>With a name, a list containing land_cols and sea_cols. Without a
name, a named list of those pairs.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/dem-palettes.R`. [Full function help](help/demPalettes.html) · [Terrain horizons and panoramas outline](contents-plan.html#plan-terrain) · [Generating a terrain panorama](horizons.html#sec-dem-panorama)

### `downloadHWT()` {#fn-downloadhwt}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-downloadhwt)

```{=html}
<p>A panorama describes the horizon seen from a particular observer location. The
optional httr2 package retrieves site metadata and 0.125-degree horizon bins over
HTTPS. Site elevation above sea level is reported in metres, converting feet
when necessary. Validated profiles are cached by panorama identifier for the R
session. Read-only downloads allow up to three attempts for transient HTTP
failures, with a 30-second limit per request. For each bin, the distance and
angular altitude determine a height difference. The mean angular change for
height offsets of plus and minus 9.73 metres estimates altitude uncertainty.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p><a href="https://www.heywhatsthat.com/">HeyWhatsThat.com</a>
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Separate where a provider actually placed its viewpoint from the coordinate in the request. Record the downloaded profile, reference direction and acquisition date. A provider comparison can mix terrain-source and algorithm differences.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>HWTID</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>This is the 8 character ID attributed by
<em>HeyWhatsThat.com</em></p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.horizon list containing site metadata and horizon samples. The data columns az, alt and alt.unc are in degrees. Retrieval requires access to the HeyWhatsThat service.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/horizon.R`. [Full function help](help/downloadHWT.html) · [Terrain horizons and panoramas outline](contents-plan.html#plan-terrain) · [Field reduction and survey identifiers](field-reduction.html#field-solar)

### `exportHor()` {#fn-exporthor}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-exporthor)

```{=html}
<p>A landscape lets the same terrain obstruction be used in a planetarium reconstruction.
The export pairs the profile's azimuth and altitude samples in a polygonal horizon file
and records the site, appearance and attribution in a Stellarium configuration. The
export describes the horizon geometry; the altitude-uncertainty series remains in the R
object.
</p>
<p>DEM and SVG panoramas use a spherical landscape with the PNG rotated -90
degrees for Stellarium's east-origin mapping. A new PeakFinder import also
records the original ZIP location. If native tiles are requested and that archive still matches its checksum
and contains the supported calibrated eight-tile landscape, Stellarium uses
those original textures and their angular settings instead. The export also
includes the skyscapeR numerical profile and SVG-derived PNG.
exportStellarium is an alias for exportHor.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p><a href="https://stellarium.org/guide/">Stellarium User Guide</a>, chapter on landscapes and texture sizes.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Retain the original photograph and angular controls. Re-encoding a panorama or successfully relinking its image does not independently verify its north direction, its vertical calibration or the coordinate assigned to the observer.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Horizon data in <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> format.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Horizon name to be displayed in <em>Stellarium</em>, if different
from one in <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>author</code></th><td><code>&quot;skyscapeR&quot;</code></td><td><p>Author, to be included in <em>landscape.ini</em> file.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>description</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Description, to be included in <em>landscape.ini</em> file.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>use.image</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Include a valid external panorama PNG when available. Default TRUE.
Missing or changed files warn and use a polygonal horizon instead.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>peakfinder.layout</code></th><td><code>c(&quot;single&quot;, &quot;native&quot;)</code></td><td><p>Single spherical PNG (default) or original native tiles. Textured DEM and PeakFinder exports use their PNG silhouette.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>max.texture.width</code></th><td><code>4096</code></td><td><p>Maximum exported DEM or photographic panorama width in pixels. The default is 4096. Use max.texture.width=2048 for a smaller texture, or Inf to keep the original dimensions. Stellarium supports textures only up to the graphics hardware limit. PNG compression does not reduce the decoded texture dimensions. Larger exports are at your own risk and may fail to load or crash Stellarium. This setting does not resize PeakFinder textures.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>ground_col</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Color of ground. Defaults to <em>Stellarium</em>'s default.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor_col</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Colour of a polygonal horizon line. Textured DEM and PeakFinder landscapes omit this line.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Invisibly, the absolute path of the created ZIP archive.
</p>
```

### `exportPanorama()` {#fn-exportpanorama}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-exportpanorama)

```{=html}
<p>The left edge is true north. Azimuth increases clockwise through east,
south and west. The top is the zenith, the middle is zero altitude and the
bottom is the nadir. Image exports preserve the calibrated angular bounds and
sample source pixels by nearest neighbour. Sky and areas outside photographic
coverage are transparent. For a numerical skyline, the ground extends to the
nadir over the measured azimuth sector. A missing or modified image triggers
a warning and the numerical silhouette is exported instead.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Retain the original photograph and angular controls. Re-encoding a panorama or successfully relinking its image does not independently verify its north direction, its vertical calibration or the coordinate assigned to the observer.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A skyscapeR.horizon object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>file</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Destination PNG filename. Choose a new filename for each export.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>width</code></th><td><code>4096</code></td><td><p>Even output width in pixels. Height is half the width. Default 4096.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>use.image</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Use the attached terrain or photographic texture when available.
Set FALSE to export the numerical skyline as a silhouette.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col.ground</code></th><td><code>&quot;darkgreen&quot;</code></td><td><p>Fill colour for a numerical silhouette.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>The absolute PNG path, invisibly.
</p>
```

</details>

### `hor2alt()` {#fn-hor2alt}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-hor2alt)

```{=html}
<p>For a horizon constructed from measurements or a DEM, cubic splines interpolate altitude and recorded uncertainty at the requested azimuth. For an imported photograph the function wraps bearings relative to the coverage origin, linearly interpolates its skyline and returns missing values outside its observed sector. Values are rounded to two decimal places. One bearing with uncertainty returns a numeric pair; multiple bearings with uncertainty return a matrix. Keep these routes distinct from the interpolation inside coordtrans().</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** The returned extremum or altitude depends on the supplied skyline and the bearings searched. A sharp local notch can be missed between measurements; a wider numerical search cannot recover terrain absent from the profile.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object from which to retrieve horizon altitude.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Array of azimuth(s) for which to retrieve horizon altitude(s).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>return.unc</code></th><td><code>F</code></td><td><p>Logical controlling whether to return altitude uncertainty.
Default is <em>FALSE</em>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>With <code>return.unc = FALSE</code>, a numeric vector of altitudes.
With <code>return.unc = TRUE</code> and one azimuth, an unnamed numeric vector
containing altitude followed by uncertainty. With multiple azimuths, a
numeric matrix with columns <code>alt</code> and <code>alt.unc</code>, one row per
input azimuth in the supplied order. Values are rounded to two decimal places.
</p>
```

</details>

### `horFeature()` {#fn-horfeature}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-horfeature)

```{=html}
<p>Reconstructions are explicit hypotheses about additional relief above
the supplied terrain. Heights are added to the existing DEM, including any
surviving remains already represented there. Ditch depths are subtracted.
No original ground surface or historical height is inferred. Zero height or
depth highlights a footprint without changing elevation.
</p>
<p>Every feature and multipart component is used. Points become circular
footprints with the supplied diameter. Lines become strips with half the width
on each side and round ends. Polygons use their whole area by default for
stones, poles, mounds and platforms, and their boundary for banks, ditches and
walls. Polygon holes remain holes in area mode; boundary mode includes their
edges. Dimensions are metres in a local azimuthal equidistant projection.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** A feature height is additional relief on the supplied surface. A bank can be visible below the terrain skyline, so inspect the numerical profile and panorama separately. The [H01](study-register.qmd#h01-field-validation) field residuals quantify agreement at surveyed terrain bearings. Reconstructed features need their own reference measurements.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>geometry</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A vector filename (including a shapefile or GeoPackage), a
terra SpatVector, or an object accepted by terra::vect, with a known CRS.
A layer must contain one geometry family: points, lines or polygons.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>type</code></th><td><code>c(&quot;stone&quot;, &quot;pole&quot;, &quot;bank&quot;, &quot;ditch&quot;, &quot;mound&quot;, &quot;platform&quot;, &quot;wall&quot;)</code></td><td><p>Structure type: stone, pole, bank, ditch, mound, platform or wall.
Stones and poles accept points or polygons; mounds and platforms require
polygons; banks, ditches and walls accept lines or polygons.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>height</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Additional height in metres, nonnegative. Default 0. Ignored
for ditches, which use depth. Positive height and depth cannot be combined.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>height_field</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional
attribute column names supplying per-row settings. Do not also supply the
corresponding common value. Numeric fields must be numeric, finite and meet
the same bounds as common values. Colour fields must contain valid colours.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>depth</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Nonnegative ditch depth in metres. Default 0; only for ditches.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>depth_field</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional
attribute column names supplying per-row settings. Do not also supply the
corresponding common value. Numeric fields must be numeric, finite and meet
the same bounds as common values. Colour fields must contain valid colours.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>width</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Total width in metres for lines or polygon boundaries.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>width_field</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional
attribute column names supplying per-row settings. Do not also supply the
corresponding common value. Numeric fields must be numeric, finite and meet
the same bounds as common values. Colour fields must contain valid colours.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>diameter</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Diameter in metres for point footprints.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>diameter_field</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional
attribute column names supplying per-row settings. Do not also supply the
corresponding common value. Numeric fields must be numeric, finite and meet
the same bounds as common values. Colour fields must contain valid colours.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>profile</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Either bell or flat. Defaults to bell for banks, ditches and
mounds, and flat for stones, poles, platforms and walls.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>use</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>For polygons, area or boundary. NULL chooses the type's default.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>colour</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>One opaque R colour, or NULL for the terrain palette.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>colour_field</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional
attribute column names supplying per-row settings. Do not also supply the
corresponding common value. Numeric fields must be numeric, finite and meet
the same bounds as common values. Colour fields must contain valid colours.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Descriptive label for the layer. Defaults to the structure type.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. ### `importPanorama()` {#fn-importpanorama}
```

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-importpanorama)

```{=html}
<p>Choose controls according to what you know:
</p>
<p>The picker samples the overview. Choose Zoom and click two corners to display the selected region at native pixel detail, then choose Add control point. Full-turn plots cut the calibrated view at north. In scripted controls use <code>NA_real_</code> for each unknown angle. Levelling adjusts the near-horizon band. If an altitude shift takes image rows beyond the poles, only whole rows within the physical altitude range are kept. A one-point adjustment records the calibrated bounds and uses the original PNG. Keep it with the saved object. A tilt adjustment writes a levelled PNG in the working directory. Use a panorama with nominally linear angular axes and transparent sky above terrain in every column. A partial panorama supports altitude lookup within its photographed sector. Stellarium export requires a full turn.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Retain the original photograph and angular controls. Re-encoding a panorama or successfully relinking its image does not independently verify its north direction, its vertical calibration or the coordinate assigned to the observer.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>file</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>PNG with sky removed to transparency. Keep this file alongside saved horizon objects.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>WGS84 latitude, longitude and optional elevation in metres.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>az.lim</code></th><td><code>c(0, 360)</code></td><td><p>True bearings of the left and right edges, increasing clockwise. A sector may cross north, e.g. c(330,30).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt.lim</code></th><td><code>c(-90, 90)</code></td><td><p>Altitudes of the bottom and top edges in degrees. Set these explicitly for a cropped panorama.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td><code>tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))</code></td><td><p>Site name.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calibrate</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>Open the interactive graphics picker. Choose Zoom and click two corners to enlarge a region. Add a control by clicking a landmark and entering its true azimuth, altitude or both. Finish to apply the fit.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>points</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional data frame with numeric x, y, az and alt. Pixel coordinates start at the upper-left image edge. Use NA for an unknown angle.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alpha.threshold</code></th><td><code>0.5</code></td><td><p>Minimum opacity counted as terrain, from above zero to one.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt.unc</code></th><td><code>0.5</code></td><td><p>Assumed skyline altitude uncertainty in degrees.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.horizon object with a numerical profile, external PNG reference, angular bounds and control points. Use saveRDS() to save the object. Copy the displayed panorama PNG with the RDS and use <code>relinkHor</code> to reconnect a moved horizon or list.
</p><h5>Extraction method and limitations</h5><p>Sky detection uses the PNG alpha channel. In each image column the first pixel
whose opacity reaches <code>alpha.threshold</code> defines the terrain edge. The
function does not segment an ordinary opaque photograph by sky colour. Remove
the sky to transparency beforehand and retain sky above terrain in every column.
Trees, buildings and mask errors become part of the extracted skyline.
</p><p>Calibration uses linear angular axes, origin shifts and, where supported by
the controls, fitted scale or sinusoidal near-horizon tilt corrections.
This is not a general camera/lens model or a full spherical photogrammetric
adjustment. Wide-angle distortion, stitched-image parallax and inaccurate
control measurements are not removed automatically. The supplied
<code>alt.unc</code> is an assumed error, not an uncertainty estimated from the fit.
Inspect independent field controls after calibration.
</p><p>A partial panorama only supplies the photographed sector; it is unsuitable for
functions requiring a closed full horizon. Supplying only latitude and longitude
leaves observer elevation unknown. Add a finite measured elevation before
using functions, such as <code>sketchSky</code>, that require it.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/importPanorama.R`.
