### `importPeakFinder()` {#fn-importpeakfinder}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-importpeakfinder)

```{=html}
<p>The numerical horizon describes angular obstruction at the observer's
location. A separate vector drawing supplies foreground detail but does not
explicitly record its vertical angular calibration. Both exports are therefore
needed to create a calibrated panorama PNG. Calculations always use the numerical
horizon, never the PNG. Terrain data do not include every tree or building.
</p>
<p>In PeakFinder choose Export, Horizon for Stellarium and save the ZIP. For an
image also choose Export, SVG for printing, Silhouettes (Vector SVG), from 0
to 360 degrees, preferably picture format 16:2. Use exactly the same viewpoint
and observer height for both. Contours (Bitmap SVG) is not supported. The PNG
is a white terrain silhouette with dark foreground ridge lines and transparent
sky, without labels or shading. Only PeakFinder's untransformed M/L vector
path format is supported; edited or future formats may require adaptation.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p><a href="https://www.peakfinder.com/">PeakFinder</a>, exported drawings
attributed to PeakFinder under CC BY 4.0. Geometry conventions follow the
<a href="https://stellarium.org/guide/">Stellarium User Guide</a>.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Separate where a provider actually placed its viewpoint from the coordinate in the request. Record the downloaded profile, reference direction and acquisition date. A provider comparison can mix terrain-source and algorithm differences.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>file</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Path to a PeakFinder Stellarium ZIP export.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>svg</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional path to the matching full-circle Vector SVG export.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>elevation</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional verified absolute observer elevation in metres.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt.unc</code></th><td><code>0.5</code></td><td><p>Assumed horizon altitude uncertainty in degrees, a nonnegative scalar.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>width</code></th><td><code>4096</code></td><td><p>PNG width in pixels, an integer from 512 to 8192. Default 4096.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>image.dir</code></th><td><code>getwd()</code></td><td><p>Directory for generated PNGs; defaults to the working directory.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.horizon containing a periodically extended numerical horizon,
site and source metadata, and, on successful calibration, metadata$image with
the external PNG path, checksum, angular bounds and calibration diagnostics.
```

### `plot.skyscapeR.horizon()` {#fn-plot-skyscaper-horizon}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-plot-skyscaper-horizon)

```{=html}
<p>A track meeting the horizon identifies a possible rise or set direction for that
declination. The horizontal axis is true bearing and the vertical axis is angular
altitude. The function fills the terrain below the stored profile and can overlay
diurnal tracks computed for the observing location. Refraction affects those tracks.
Rescaling the display or changing its colours does not change the underlying horizon. Add lines or polygons in azimuth and altitude immediately after plotting. Set <code>par(mfrow=c(2,1))</code> before plotting to stack two horizons.
</p>
<p>For a two-year epoch range, draw tracks for the stored minimum and maximum
declinations, using the session refraction setting for both tracks. Line
styles are taken from the target object; older objects without them use
solid lines of width 1.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Terrain colour, shading and cropping can make a landform easier to recognise. Evaluate the profile at the archaeological bearing for a numerical claim about horizon altitude.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>x</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Object of <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> format.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.az</code></th><td><code>(!missing(xrange) || !missing(xlim))</code></td><td><p>Logical that controls whether to display azimuth values or cardinal
directions. Defaults to TRUE when xrange is supplied.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>xrange</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Azimuth range for plotting.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>yrange</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Altitude range for plotting. By default one degree of altitude occupies the same distance as one degree of azimuth on the device.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>obj</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <em>skyscapeR.object</em> from <code>skyObject</code>, or
a list of these objects. Each group retains its own epochs and styles
for displaying the paths of celestial objects.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col.ground</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Silhouette colour. NULL uses a dark muted foreground for natural skies, pale grey-green for publication colour or grey for monochrome.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col.sky</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Earlier name for a solid sky colour. Prefer sky.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>use.image</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Use an attached external panorama PNG when available. Default TRUE.
Missing or changed files warn and fall back to the numerical silhouette.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>...</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Additional arguments to be passed to <em>plot</em>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.skyline</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Draw the numerical skyline. By default the line appears only without a panorama PNG.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>sky</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>A colour string or a background from <code>sketchSky</code> or <code>stellariumSky</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>xlim</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Earlier name for xrange.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>ylim</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Earlier name for yrange.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>fastLoad</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>Use a sampled PNG for quick plots. New photographic imports store a preview. For older horizons the first preview loads the image. The numerical skyline and celestial tracks retain their precision.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.legend</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Display the key for celestial tracks. The angular axes are always drawn.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>style</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Frame and silhouette style. A sketch supplies its stored style by default. Without a
sketch the default is <code>"publication-colour"</code>. Other choices are <code>"natural"</code> and
<code>"publication-mono"</code>. Supplied panorama pixels and sky objects retain their own rendering.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Draws the horizon and returns the session atmosphere invisibly in a list.
</p><h5>Layers and coordinate consistency</h5><p>A reusable sky is calculated for its own stored location and instant. Pair it
with the horizon used to create it; drawing a saved sky does not recalculate
its positions for another observer. Celestial reference tracks from
<code>skyObject</code> use the plotted horizon's location and session
atmosphere. Keep that atmosphere consistent with the stored sketch when
comparing a track with a disc or point symbol.
</p><p>The foreground masks sky layers geometrically. It does not make the sky object
an extinction or visibility calculation through the terrain. Image calibration
and numerical skyline agreement remain the responsibility of the horizon
source. Azimuth-altitude plotting is a cylindrical display, with increasing
horizontal distortion towards the zenith. Retain consistent ranges when
comparing styles, epochs or constellation traditions.
</p>
```

### `relinkHor()` {#fn-relinkhor}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-relinkhor)

```{=html}
<p>A saved horizon records the checksum of its displayed PNG. Copy that PNG with the RDS, including the levelled copy for a calibrated photograph. Matching checks file contents, so a renamed file can be recovered and different panoramas with the same filename can be distinguished. For identical copies, the original basename is preferred, then the first matching candidate. A skyline-only horizon passes through unchanged. If any required image cannot be verified, the function stops before returning a result. Assign the returned object and use saveRDS() to keep the updated paths. The original PeakFinder archive used for native-layout export is separate.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Retain the original photograph and angular controls. Re-encoding a panorama or successfully relinking its image does not independently verify its north direction, its vertical calibration or the coordinate assigned to the observer.

Defaults to FALSE.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>The horizon or list, retaining its names, order and metadata with updated absolute PNG paths.
```{=html}
</p>
```

## From bearings to celestial targets {#group-targets}

A target search inherits the uncertainty and coordinate conventions of the original sightline. An extreme found within a restricted bearing sector is conditional on the sector searched.

### `antizenith()` {#fn-antizenith}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-antizenith)

```{=html}
<p>The direction opposite the zenith corresponds geometrically to minus the site latitude.
The function checks the site against the default-epoch solstitial latitude band,
then subtracts the approximate solar parallax correction from the negative latitude. It
returns NULL outside that band. This is a target declination for comparison with
orientations, not an observable solar transit below ground.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Record the site's latitude and the epoch and parallax assumptions used for a solar limit. A returned limit is a geometrical target; an observer still needs an independent reason to regard it as culturally significant.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>This can be either the latitude of the
location, or a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>parallax</code></th><td><code>0.00224</code></td><td><p>Mean horizontal parallax in degrees. The default is 0.00224 degrees for the Sun.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>altitude</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Altitude of the sun. Defaults to 0 degrees.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Solar declination in degrees with the requested parallax correction, or NULL when the latitude falls outside the solstitial limits used by the function.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/events.R`. [Full function help](help/antizenith.html) · [From bearings to celestial targets outline](contents-plan.html#plan-targets) · [Identifying celestial candidates and limiting declinations](celestial-targets.html#target-limits)

### `az2dec()` {#fn-az2dec}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-az2dec)

```{=html}
<p>The same true bearing can indicate different declinations when the observer or horizon
changes. Supply angular altitude directly or interpolate it from one shared horizon or
one horizon per observation. Numeric latitude inputs imply zero longitude and elevation;
a location matrix can include both. When refraction is enabled, the function adjusts the
input altitude using pressure, temperature and elevation, then calls the inverse Swiss
Ephemeris horizontal transformation. Bearings are clockwise from north; the routine
shifts them to the engine convention and rounds the returned declinations using the
input bearing representation.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** A target match inherits the skyline, epoch range and sightline uncertainty used to generate it. The number of plausible candidates also depends on catalogue coverage and the search window.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>True bearing or vector of bearings in degrees clockwise from north.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>One latitude or one per bearing (degrees north), a site matrix with one row per bearing
(latitude, longitude and optional elevation), a shared horizon or a list of horizons in measurement order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Horizon altitude in degrees, shared or one per bearing. Omit when supplying
horizons to interpolate altitude at each bearing with <code>hor2alt</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$refraction</code></td><td><p>Logical. Apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$atm</code></td><td><p>Atmospheric pressure in mbar. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$temp</code></td><td><p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Numeric declination in degrees for the supplied azimuth and altitude values.
</p>
```

</details>

### `findTargets()` {#fn-findtargets}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-findtargets)

```{=html}
<p>The search tests overlap in declination. Solar and lunar limiting declinations are
sampled across the years of the interval. Site coordinates enable zenith targets
and a horizon enables the spatial equinox. The named equinoxes and solstices use
geocentric apparent solar longitudes of 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees. Dates are UT
civil days in the requested calendar. Different dates for the first and last year
appear in endpoint order separated by a slash. Intermediate years can differ.
The sunrise/set date ranges also use the two endpoint years.
For each star passing the catalogue magnitude cut, the search computes its
declination at noon UT on 1 January Gregorian of every astronomical year,
including both endpoints. It tests overlap before rounding and linearly
interpolates between annual samples to estimate entry and exit. Separate
passages are reported separately, with boundaries rounded to the nearest year.
Shorter variations within a sampling year are unresolved. Magnitude describes
catalogue brightness and does not model atmospheric visibility.
</p>
<p>Silva and Lomsdalen (2025, table 5) give an example of stellar target screening for the Maltese temples.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Silva, F. and Lomsdalen, T. (2025). 'No easy way from the earth to the stars': a new statistical approach to the orientation of the Maltese temples. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 17, 96. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1007/s12520-025-02208-4")}.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A target match inherits the skyline, epoch range and sightline uncertainty used to generate it. The number of plausible candidates also depends on catalogue coverage and the search window.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>decrange</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Range of declination to consider.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Temporal range to consider. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>FALSE for geocentric declinations, a vector of latitude, longitude and elevation, or a skyscapeR.horizon to also evaluate the local horizon.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>max.mag</code></th><td><code>2.5</code></td><td><p>Maximum magnitude of stars to consider. Defaults to 2.5</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>dates</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>Whether to display time period when identified celestial targets
occur within declination range. Default is FALSE.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$calendar</code></td><td><p>Calendar for civil dates. Use <code>"G"</code> for Gregorian or <code>"J"</code> for Julian.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timerange</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Earlier argument name for <code>year</code>, retained for existing scripts.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A list of candidate solar, lunar and stellar matches. The tables give target names and declination limits in degrees. Stellar matches also carry catalogue identifiers and visual magnitudes. Set dates to TRUE to request stellar date ranges. A category with no matches may be absent.
</p><h5>Candidate selection and visibility</h5><p>A match is a declination overlap, not evidence that a celestial object was
visible, deliberately observed or associated with the archaeological feature.
The magnitude filter uses fixed catalogue values; it includes integrated
magnitudes for non-stellar entries such as M45. It does not predict naked-eye
visibility through extinction or twilight, or resolve the members of a cluster.
</p><p>Choose the dating interval and measurement uncertainty from the archaeological
and survey evidence. Then examine candidate stars with <code>star.phases</code>,
<code>riseset</code> and <code>sketchSky</code>. For a statistically selected
local declination band, candidate screening is exploratory; the significance
of that band does not identify its cause. Physical plausibility and independent
archaeological evidence are separate parts of the interpretation.
</p><h5>Spatial equinox epochs</h5><p>When a horizon is supplied, the spatial equinox is evaluated at both endpoints
of the requested year range (once for a single year), with the current atmospheric
settings. The candidate interval spans the finite sunrise and sunset declinations
at those endpoints. This is an endpoint envelope, not an exhaustive search for
intermediate changes of terrain crossing over very long periods. Undefined
crossings generate warnings; if all are undefined, the candidate is omitted.
</p>
```

</details>

### `hor2max.dec()` {#fn-hor2max-dec}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-hor2max-dec)

```{=html}
<p>Terrain relief can shift the limiting sightline away from the meridian. The function
samples bearings at 0.01-degree spacing within the specified half-width around 0
degrees. It calls az2dec at each bearing with the stored horizon, or with the supplied
latitude and constant altitude, then returns the maximum sampled declination. A limited
search sector may miss a more extreme sightline elsewhere.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** The returned extremum or altitude depends on the supplied skyline and the bearings searched. A sharp local notch can be missed between measurements; a wider numerical search cannot recover terrain absent from the profile.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object or the latitude of the place.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Altitude of the horizon at northernmost point. Only necessary if no
<em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object is provided. Default is 0.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>range</code></th><td><code>25</code></td><td><p>Range of azimuths to check for minimum declination. Default is 25
degrees either side of North.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>One numeric value in degrees, the largest declination sampled across the specified azimuth range around north.
</p>
```

</details>

### `orbit()` {#fn-orbit}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-orbit)

```{=html}
<p>Latitude and declination determine where a diurnal track can meet the terrain. The
function sweeps equatorial right ascension through 360 degrees at the requested angular
step and converts each position to horizontal coordinates with the selected refraction
and atmosphere settings. It retains altitudes above -20 degrees and sorts the points by
azimuth. A horizon object supplies the location; the stored track itself includes no
test of terrain obstruction or event times.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** An orbit is sampled from an idealised fixed-declination track. A spatial equinox uses site-specific solstitial crossing geometry. State which eastern or western skyline feature supports an archaeological interpretation of the midpoint.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>dec</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Declination of object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Location, either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> or a vector
containing the latitude and longitude of location, in this order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Logical. Apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Atmospheric pressure in mbar. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>res</code></th><td><code>0.25</code></td><td><p>The resolution (in degrees of RA) with which to calculate the path.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.orbit list with az and alt vectors in degrees, ordered by azimuth, plus the input declination (dec) and location (georef). The sampled track retains altitudes above -20 degrees.
</p>
```

</details>

### `sky.objects()` {#fn-sky-objects}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-sky-objects)

```{=html}
<p>An overlay identifies which targets to compare before inspecting a distribution. Names
may denote stars, solar or lunar limits, or fixed custom declinations. Group names
expand into the individual limits. At one epoch, the function evaluates each target; for
two endpoints it uses annual January stellar declinations. Solar and lunar limits
retain century-spaced samples and spline interpolation. Styles and epoch travel with the object. Treat range endpoints as
model estimates and verify narrow or rapidly changing windows separately.
A single object can contain several related targets. Pass a list of objects
to plot(hor), plotBars or plotAzimuth to combine groups with independent
epochs, colours, line styles and labels. Groups are drawn in list order.
Horizon plots use the plotted horizon's location for every track. Compass
plots use each group's stored location and a level horizon, drawing both
declination boundaries for a year-range group. Declination plots need no
location. No common epoch range is imposed and no astronomical positions
are recomputed merely by combining objects. The output class remains
skyscapeR.object, so previously saved objects remain usable.
sky.objects is a silent compatibility alias for skyObject.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Overlays help compare specified targets with an orientation distribution. Selecting overlays after viewing a peak introduces a search across targets outside the local adjustment in the significance test.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>names</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Target names, star names or custom declinations in degrees. Use "solar extremes" for the solstices or "lunar extremes" for the four lunar extremes.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>An astronomical year or a pair of year endpoints. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>This can be either a vector with the latitude and longitude of the
location, or a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col</code></th><td><code>&quot;#A9542E&quot;</code></td><td><p>The color for plotting, and differentiating these objects.
Defaults to ochre for all objects.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>lty</code></th><td><code>1</code></td><td><p>Line type (see <code>par</code>) used for differentiation.
Used for single-year tracks and year-range boundaries.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>lwd</code></th><td><code>1</code></td><td><p>Line width (see <code>par</code>) used for differentiation.
Used for single-year tracks and year-range boundaries.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>epoch</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Earlier argument name for <code>year</code>, retained for existing scripts.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.object list. Columns of decs represent targets, in degrees. A single epoch produces one row. For a two-year range the rows are labelled min and max. The other fields record target count, epoch, location and plotting styles.
</p><h5>A reference track is not a dated orbit</h5><p>Each target represents a declination or declination range. A plotted track
holds that declination fixed while hour angle varies. It does not follow the
changing declination of a moving Solar System body through a particular day.
In particular, <code>skyObject("Equinox", year)</code> is an equinox reference;
the Sun at sunrise or sunset on the equinox date need not lie at the same
declination as at the equinox instant. A small offset from a solar disc in
<code>sketchSky</code> can therefore be expected.
</p><p>To compare with a particular instant, obtain its declination with
<code>body.position</code> using the intended coordinate frame, and pass
that numeric value to <code>skyObject</code>. Even that fixed-declination track is
an approximation to a moving body's full daily orbit. Refraction and the
plotted site's coordinates are applied when drawing the horizon track.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/events.R`. [Full function help](help/skyObject.html) · [From bearings to celestial targets outline](contents-plan.html#plan-targets) · [Identifying celestial candidates and limiting declinations](celestial-targets.html#target-overlay)

### `spatial.equinox()` {#fn-spatial-equinox}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-spatial-equinox)

```{=html}
<p>A spatial midpoint is defined by the local terrain and need not coincide with the
astronomical equinox. The function uses the positive and negative obliquity at
the requested year as the geocentric solstitial declinations. Each fixed track
is followed through one rotation from lower culmination to lower culmination.
Horizontal solar parallax is applied to geometric altitude before atmospheric
refraction. The terrain is interpolated linearly in azimuth.
</p>
<p>On the rising half of each track, the first emergence is selected; on the
setting half, the final disappearance is selected. The circular midpoint of
the two solstitial bearings is then found separately for sunrise and sunset.
At each midpoint, refraction and horizontal parallax are inverted to recover
the geocentric declination. Atmospheric settings are identical in both stages.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Ruggles, C. L. N. (1997). Whose Equinox? Journal for the History of Astronomy 28, S45-S96. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182869702802205")}.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** An orbit is sampled from an idealised fixed-declination track. A spatial equinox uses site-specific solstitial crossing geometry. State which eastern or western skyline feature supports an archaeological interpretation of the midpoint.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> with finite, increasing azimuths covering
0 to 360 degrees and matching endpoint altitudes.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>parallax</code></th><td><code>0.00224</code></td><td><p>Mean horizontal parallax in degrees. The default is 0.00224 degrees for the Sun.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$cur.year</code></td><td><p>One astronomical year, defaulting to the package's current-year
setting. Historical labels such as <code>"3250 BC"</code> are accepted.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$refraction</code></td><td><p>Whether to apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the
package setting, normally TRUE.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$atm</code></td><td><p>Atmospheric pressure in hPa. Defaults to the package setting.
Zero requests an estimate from site elevation.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$temp</code></td><td><p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the package setting.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A list containing azimuth and declination. Each contains rise and set
values in degrees for the supplied horizon. Declinations are geocentric.
An undefined side returns NA for both values, with a warning; the other side
is retained when defined.
</p><h5>Crossing conventions and limitations</h5><p>Both rising and setting tracks are considered in either hemisphere. The
search uses the terrain-aware crossing machinery also used by
<code>riseset</code>, including terrain vertices and interior extrema.
Tangencies without a change of visibility are excluded. Multiple terrain
crossings are resolved using the first-emergence/final-disappearance rule;
this need not be the locally preferred observational definition of sunrise
or sunset. Inspect complex skylines before interpretation.
</p><p>If either solstitial track lacks the required crossing, the corresponding
midpoint is undefined. This includes polar non-rising/non-setting cases and
complete terrain obstruction. Exactly opposite bearings have no unique
circular midpoint and also return NA.
</p><p>These are fixed-declination solar-centre tracks, not a dated solar ephemeris
or upper-limb calculation. The mean horizontal parallax is fixed, and the
refraction model cannot represent local atmospheric anomalies. Results are
limited by horizon resolution and atmospheric assumptions. Solar semidiameter
is not included. The result is a spatial midpoint, not the Sun's rising or
setting at the astronomical equinox.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/events.R`. ### `zenith()` {#fn-zenith}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-zenith)

```{=html}
<p>The geometric zenith has declination equal to the site latitude. The function
first checks the latitude against its June and December solar limits at the default
epoch. Within those limits it subtracts the supplied approximate solar parallax
correction from the latitude. It returns NULL outside the permitted band. This supplies
a declination criterion rather than the dates of the passages.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Record the site's latitude and the epoch and parallax assumptions used for a solar limit. A returned limit is a geometrical target; an observer still needs an independent reason to regard it as culturally significant.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>This can be either the latitude of the
location, or a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>parallax</code></th><td><code>0.00224</code></td><td><p>Mean horizontal parallax in degrees. The default is 0.00224 degrees for the Sun.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>altitude</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Altitude of the sun. Defaults to 0 degrees.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Solar declination in degrees with the requested parallax correction, or NULL when the latitude falls outside the solstitial limits used by the function.
</p>
```

</details>

## Solar, lunar and planetary events {#group-events}

Distinguish a geocentric extreme from a topocentric crossing on a particular civil date. Numerical precision in the event search does not fix an uncertain horizon or observer position.

### `CC()` {#fn-cc}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-cc)

```{=html}
<p>Crescent crossovers describe a change in the relative horizon positions
of the luminaries across successive lunations. First (waxing) crescents are
compared at sunset and moonset; last (waning) crescents at sunrise and moonrise.
The method follows Silva and Pimenta (2012), sections 2.1–2.2. Seasons use the
paper's northern-hemisphere names: summer means the June-solstice crossover,
winter the December-solstice crossover, also for southern-hemisphere locations.
</p>
<p>For each conjunction, days are searched forwards for the first crescent and
backwards for the last crescent. Visibility is evaluated at sunset or sunrise,
respectively, using Caldwell and Laney's criterion: lower-limb lunar altitude
plus one third of the Sun–Moon angular separation must be at least 11.3 degrees.
The lower-limb altitude is topocentric. The arc of light is the geocentric
Sun–Moon separation, as explicitly defined by Caldwell and Laney; it excludes
atmospheric refraction. The lower limb is calculated from the instantaneous lunar distance
and a lunar radius of 1737.4 km. With refraction enabled, the centre altitude is
apparent and the angular radius is subtracted from it. This is an empirical
visibility prediction, not a guarantee under actual weather or extinction.
</p>
```

**Comparison with the original simulations.**

```{=html}
<p>For SIM1, 5,024 of 5,136 events in the supplied 1620–2047 series at
latitudes 0, 60 N and 60 S agree within 0.02 degrees in lunar declination.
This comparison uses a level horizon, longitude 0, elevation 400 m, UTC,
Gregorian dates, refraction, pressure 1013.25 mbar and temperature 15 degrees
Celsius. The original 40-degree N series has additional systematic offsets.
Of the 112 discrepancies outside that series, inferred matching dates suggest
differences in the lunation search window and first/last crescent selection.
Some lie close to the visibility threshold. Alternative window and solar-limb
conventions improve some cases but disrupt others that already agree, so no
replacement convention has been adopted. The exact original settings remain
unresolved; the paper does not specify all atmospheric inputs. Inspect the
diagnostics before interpreting individual events. Agreement with simulation
tables is not independent observational validation, and these SIM1 counts do
not establish the accuracy of SIM2.
</p>



```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Silva, F. and Pimenta, F. (2012). The Crossover of the Sun and the
Moon. Journal for the History of Astronomy 43(2), 191–208.
\Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182861204300204")}.
</p>
<p>Caldwell, J. and Laney, C. D. (2001). First visibility of the lunar crescent.
African Skies 5, 15–23. The authors' online version defines dalt and arcl:
<a href="https://astronomycenter.net/pdf/saao_2001.pdf">https://astronomycenter.net/pdf/saao_2001.pdf</a>.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** The event-selection rules include ordered conditions across solar and lunar events. Use the recorded diagnostics to identify the first condition that differs when comparing with the Silva and Pimenta simulations. A similar terminal azimuth does not establish identical event selection.

### `dS()` {#fn-ds}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-ds)

```{=html}
<p>The December solstice is represented by the negative obliquity of the ecliptic for the
requested epoch. The result is geocentric when no site is supplied. With a site, the
function subtracts the approximate parallax correction using latitude and target
altitude. This obliquity-based target does not determine a solstice time or a sunrise or
sunset bearing.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** A target constructed from obliquity or a zero equinoctial declination answers a different question from dating a crossing. For a near-horizon observation report whether the calculation includes the local parallax adjustment.

### `EFM()` {#fn-efm}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-efm)

```{=html}
<p>Silva and Pimenta (2012) identify the crossover by the first near-full
Moon on the seasonal side of the Sun. Spring and autumn refer to the March
and September equinoxes. At spring moonrise the lunar azimuth must exceed
the solar azimuth, and at spring moonset it must be smaller. Autumn reverses
both inequalities. Bearings are topocentric, clockwise from north.
</p>
<p>The search runs chronologically from 60 days before to 65 days after the
astronomical equinox. Moonrise is paired with the first sunrise on the same
local civil date. Moonset is paired with the most recent sunset before it,
considering the first solar centre crossing on the current and preceding
local civil dates. A candidate without such a sunset is skipped. Local-day
boundaries account for timezone changes, including daylight saving time.
A coordinate vector
specifies a level horizon. A horizon object supplies the horizon for both
bodies. Illumination is tested at the lunar event itself. A date qualifies
as soon as the illumination and strict bearing conditions both hold. A
lower illumination threshold can select an earlier lunation. If no date
qualifies the function reports the year and event and stops.
</p>
```

**Comparison with the original simulations.**

```{=html}
<p>With the corrected preceding-sunset pairing, 2,562 of 2,568 moonsets in
the supplied 1620–2047 series at latitudes 0, 60 N and 60 S agree within
0.02 degrees in lunar declination. The comparison uses a level horizon,
longitude 0, elevation 400 m, UTC, Gregorian dates, geocentric declinations,
refraction, pressure 1013.25 mbar, temperature 15 degrees Celsius and the
default illumination threshold. Five remaining cases lie just above the
0.99 illumination boundary; one lies about 0.002 degrees beyond the azimuth
crossover boundary. The original series selects the following morning in
each case. Thresholds have not been tuned to reproduce those selections.
</p>
<p>The original 40-degree N series retains systematic coordinate differences.
Diagnostic comparisons suggest a different coordinate-conversion or timing
convention, but the original settings have not been established. Agreement
with these simulation tables is not independent observational validation.
The paper does not specify all atmospheric settings; the values above describe
this comparison, not confirmed settings of the original simulations.
</p>
<p>Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing <span class="pkg">swephRdata</span>; see <code>skyscapeR-package</code> for setup.
</p>



```

**Scope of the event model.**

```{=html}
<p>The illumination fraction is a selection criterion, not a naked-eye detection
model. The calculation does not include weather, sky brightness or extinction.
It uses centre crossings rather than the first appearance of the upper limb.
Only the first qualifying event is returned, so changes in illumination
threshold, civil-day convention or horizon can change the selected lunation.
Remaining differences from the original simulations are described above.
Numerical precision does not establish agreement with a published distribution.
Preserve all inputs when comparing series.
</p>



```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Silva, F. and Pimenta, F. (2012). The Crossover of the Sun and the Moon. Journal for the History of Astronomy 43. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182861204300204")}.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** The event-selection rules include ordered conditions across solar and lunar events. Use the recorded diagnostics to identify the first condition that differs when comparing with the Silva and Pimenta simulations. A similar terminal azimuth does not establish identical event selection.

Can be either a single value (the year), Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.
```{=html}
two values (range of years), or a vector of years.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>This can be either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object, or a vector with the
```

### `eq()` {#fn-eq}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-eq)

```{=html}
<p>The geometric reference at an equinox is the celestial equator, with geocentric
declination zero. Supplying a location subtracts the package's approximate parallax
correction for the latitude and specified altitude. The result is a declination target
in degrees; no equinox date, event time or horizon crossing is calculated.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** A target constructed from obliquity or a zero equinoctial declination answers a different question from dating a crossing. For a near-horizon observation report whether the calculation includes the local parallax adjustment.

### `moonphase()` {#fn-moonphase}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-moonphase)

```{=html}
<p>Lunar illumination can be used to screen events for a nearly full Moon. The routine
converts calendar input to UT Julian dates when needed and obtains the illuminated
fraction from the lunar phenomena calculation in Swiss Ephemeris. Values near zero
indicate a nearly new Moon and values near one a nearly full Moon; the fraction alone
cannot distinguish waxing from waning.
</p>
<p>Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing <span class="pkg">swephRdata</span>; see <code>skyscapeR-package</code> for setup.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Illuminated fraction alone supplies no brightness or atmospheric detection criterion. A planetary extreme is conditional on its sampled time window and cadence. Retain that window when comparing extremes between studies.

```{=html}

Use UTC or a fixed offset for dates before 1900. See <code>time2jd</code> for named zones and offsets.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Calendar for civil dates. Use <code>"G"</code> for Gregorian or <code>"J"</code> for Julian.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Numeric illuminated fraction of the lunar disc, one value per input time. At full illumination the fraction is 1.
</p>
```

### `nMjLX()` {#fn-nmjlx}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-nmjlx)

```{=html}
<p>A major standstill defines a limiting lunar declination at the epoch of interest. The
model uses the obliquity plus a fixed 5.145 + 0.145 degrees, then applies the positive
sign for the northern limit. With a location it subtracts the parallax correction for
latitude and altitude. The default lunar parallax is 0.952 degrees. This approximation
defines a target limit; it does not search a time series for an actual lunar event.
</p>
<p>Sprajc (2016) describes the limits set by obliquity and the mean lunar
inclination. This package also includes the fixed 0.145-degree term above.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Šprajc, I. (2016). Lunar alignments in Mesoamerican architecture. Anthropological Notebooks 22(3), 61-85.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A standstill envelope gives a target limit. To compare with a particular observed Moon, compute its topocentric position at the instant and test the local skyline separately.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.env$cur.year</code></td><td><p>Astronomical year. The default is the current year in the package settings. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>Latitude in degrees north or a <code>skyscapeR.horizon</code> object. Omit this argument or use <code>FALSE</code> for geocentric declination.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>parallax</code></th><td><code>0.952</code></td><td><p>Mean horizontal parallax in degrees. The default is 0.952 degrees for the Moon.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>altitude</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>Altitude of the Moon. Defaults to 0 degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Logical to control output of warnings and messages.
Defaults to TRUE.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Numeric declination in degrees. With loc = FALSE the result is geocentric. Supplying a location applies the parallax correction for the chosen altitude.
</p>
```

</details>

```{=html}
model uses the obliquity minus a fixed 5.145 + 0.145 degrees, then applies the positive
sign for the northern limit. With a location it subtracts the parallax correction for

</p>

inclination. This package also includes the fixed 0.145-degree term above.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Šprajc, I. (2016). Lunar alignments in Mesoamerican architecture. Anthropological Notebooks 22(3), 61-85.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A standstill envelope gives a target limit. To compare with a particular observed Moon, compute its topocentric position at the instant and test the local skyline separately.

### `planet.extremes()` {#fn-planet-extremes}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-planet-extremes)

```{=html}
<p>An epoch alone does not specify the planet's position in its cycle. The search extends
three quarters of the package's planet-specific period on either side of the epoch,
rounds the limiting years, and samples at daily intervals from noon UT on 1 January of
the start year to the corresponding date in the end year. Each sample uses body.position
and the requested site if supplied. The returned extrema are the range of these samples;
finer extrema can fall between sampled instants.
</p>
<p>Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing <span class="pkg">swephRdata</span>; see <code>skyscapeR-package</code> for setup.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Illuminated fraction alone supplies no brightness or atmospheric detection criterion. A planetary extreme is conditional on its sampled time window and cadence. Retain that window when comparing extremes between studies.

Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>This can be either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> object, or a vector with the
```{=html}
latitude, longitude and elevation of the site, in this order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>epoch</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Earlier argument name for <code>year</code>, retained for existing scripts.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A list containing planet, min.dec and max.dec. The two declinations are extrema of daily samples and are expressed in degrees.
</p>
```

### `riseset()` {#fn-riseset}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-riseset)

```{=html}
<p>The event is a crossing of the local horizon by the body's centre. A raised ridge can
delay the first visible rise and an uneven horizon can give several appearances or
disappearances. Choose the horizon model, atmosphere, calendar and time convention to
match the observation.
</p>
<p>Events refer to the centre of the disc. For a Solar System body with a coordinate vector, alt is
one constant horizon altitude and the Swiss Ephemeris rise/set solver is used.
For stars, the daily track is evaluated against the supplied constant altitude or site skyline. With a horizon object, its profile is linearly interpolated in azimuth and
compared with the body's topocentric altitude; do not supply alt as well.
Refraction TRUE uses apparent altitude; FALSE uses geometric altitude. The
constant-altitude solver likewise disables refraction only when FALSE.
For a profile, search the 48 hours after each requested local midnight and
return the first upward and first downward crossing separately. They need
not enclose one continuous visibility interval or occur on the requested day.
Missing crossings return NA fields. A one-minute base grid, quarter-step samples,
azimuth turning points and recursively subdivided rapid azimuth motion bracket visits
to the profile's corners. Each smooth segment is also searched for an interior altitude
extremum, so short emergence/reoccultation pairs need not straddle time samples.
A pure tangency without a sign change is not a rise or set. Horizon altitudes at
0 and 360 degrees must agree. Root tolerance is 0.01 seconds; interior optimization
uses relative seconds to avoid precision loss from large Julian dates.
These settings are not a physical accuracy guarantee: finite precision, unresolved
terrain and near-zenith azimuth singularities limit numerical completeness. The dec argument
controls returned declination, not the topocentric event search.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Astrodienst. Swiss Ephemeris programmer's manual. <a href="https://www.astro.com/swisseph/swephprg.htm">https://www.astro.com/swisseph/swephprg.htm</a>.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** An event time is conditional on the chosen event definition and clock. A centre crossing of terrain differs from first visibility of a limb; a recurring solar declination can admit more than one date.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Location, either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> or a vector
containing the latitude, longitude and elevation of location, in this order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>date</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Either a string containing the date in the format "YYYY/MM/DD"
(see <code>timestring</code>), or a numeric containing the julian date (see <code>time2jd</code>).
Can also be a single year ("YYYY") or a month ("YYYY/MM") to calculate risings and settings for every day in the
year or month, respectively. Not necessary if <em>jd</em> is given.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>jd</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A numeric containing the julian date (see <code>time2jd</code>) for which to
calculate rising and settings. Only needed if <em>date</em> is not given.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>obj</code></th><td><code>&quot;sun&quot;</code></td><td><p>Solar System body, Western star name or fixed-star catalogue identifier (including M 45). Defaults to 'sun'.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>The altitude of the horizon to consider. Defaults to zero degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Timezone for civil timestamps. Use UTC or a fixed offset for dates before 1900. See <code>time2jd</code> for named zones and offsets.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Calendar for civil dates. Use <code>"G"</code> for Gregorian or <code>"J"</code> for Julian.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>dec</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Output declination: <em>geo</em> for the geocentric, or <em>topo</em> for the topocentric
frame of reference. If not given the value set by <code>skyscapeR.vars</code> will be used instead.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Logical. Apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Atmospheric pressure in mbar. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Logical. Display progress or informational messages. Default <code>TRUE</code>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A list containing object, rise and set; rise/set are data frames
with date, time, azimuth and declination columns. Missing events have NA fields.
</p><h5>Crossing is not first visibility</h5><p>The result supplies geometry and time. It applies neither atmospheric extinction
nor a twilight detection threshold and does not test whether the star can be
seen. A centre exactly at the skyline can remain obscured in a plot or too faint
to detect. Use <code>star.phases</code> to select a candidate season, then
inspect moments after the crossing with <code>sketchSky</code> and
<code>skyStep</code>. The extra time needed for clearance depends on track
slope, latitude and terrain; a universal minute offset is inappropriate.
</p><p>A numerical root tolerance describes the solver, not observational timing
accuracy. Uncertain terrain height, refraction and ancient Earth-rotation
models can dominate it. Saved output contains formatted civil times rather
than a complete record of the input atmosphere and horizon. Preserve the
original call and convert date/time back with matching calendar and timezone.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/mechanics.R`. ### `sMjLX()` {#fn-smjlx}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-smjlx)

```{=html}
<p>A major standstill defines a limiting lunar declination at the epoch of interest. The
model uses the obliquity plus a fixed 5.145 + 0.145 degrees, then applies the negative
sign for the southern limit. With a location it subtracts the parallax correction for
latitude and altitude. The default lunar parallax is 0.952 degrees. This approximation
defines a target limit; it does not search a time series for an actual lunar event.
</p>
<p>Sprajc (2016) describes the limits set by obliquity and the mean lunar
inclination. This package also includes the fixed 0.145-degree term above.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Šprajc, I. (2016). Lunar alignments in Mesoamerican architecture. Anthropological Notebooks 22(3), 61-85.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A standstill envelope gives a target limit. To compare with a particular observed Moon, compute its topocentric position at the instant and test the local skyline separately.

Omit this argument or use <code>FALSE</code> for geocentric declination.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>parallax</code></th><td><code>0.952</code></td><td><p>Mean horizontal parallax in degrees. ### `solar.date()` {#fn-solar-date}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-solar-date)

```{=html}
<p>The Sun can pass the same declination on either side of a solstice. The search
covers the selected civil year from midnight UT, including its first instant and
excluding the start of the next year. Daily geocentric apparent solar declinations
bracket the annual turning points. The function refines each extremum against the
ephemeris and solves separately on either side, then reports the civil day of each
crossing. A tangency gives one date. Two crossings can share a calendar day.
The calculation uses no terrain or solar limb model.
</p>
<p>Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing <span class="pkg">swephRdata</span>; see <code>skyscapeR-package</code> for setup.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** An event time is conditional on the chosen event definition and clock. A centre crossing of terrain differs from first visibility of a limb; a recurring solar declination can admit more than one date.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>dec</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>One or more declinations in degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Year for which to do calculations. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Calendar for sampling and output. G for Gregorian or J for Julian. Defaults to the package calendar, initially Gregorian.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Logical. Display progress or informational messages. Default <code>TRUE</code>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A character matrix with one column per reachable input, in input order. The rows
are Dec, Date1 and Date2, with Date3 added if three passages fall in one civil
year. Dates are chronological day/month labels. Unused date cells are missing.
The function stops if all requested declinations are unreachable.
</p>
```

</details>

## Stellar positions and seasonal visibility {#group-stars}

Catalogue epoch, atmosphere, skyline and a threshold-based visibility definition enter at different stages. A representative seasonal date is distinct from the time spent above the ridge on that morning.

### `plot.skyscapeR.starphases()` {#fn-plot-skyscaper-starphases}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-plot-skyscaper-starphases)

```{=html}
<p>Read each colour as a daily model classification: visible rising and setting, rising
only, setting only, visible without a qualifying near-horizon passage, or invisible. The
function plots the stored phase sequence on a 365-day scale and can label seasons or
display a legend. A single result defaults to a circular view, advancing clockwise
from December solstice. Further results use concentric rings with one leader per displayed layer;
optional sorting uses the stored apparent magnitude or seasonal onset. Changing the
display does not recalculate the visibility thresholds. Use <code>plot(first, list(second, third))</code> to compare results.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Track clearance, seasonal visibility and the representative Julian date are different outputs. Month and phase labels organise the cycle; deciding whether a star could be detected requires a time interval above the actual skyline.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>x</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A star phase result.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>y</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A second object of <em>skyscapeR.starphases</em> format or
a list of <em>skyscapeR.starphases</em> objects for plotting (see Examples).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.labels</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Logical. Mark annual events for a single result in either layout. Defaults to TRUE.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.legend</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Show a legend for seasons present among the plotted
stars (default TRUE). For circular plots FALSE also hides titles, site/epoch text and all layer or event callouts. The seasonal scale stays visible. Linear plots keep their data and event labels.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.grid</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Draw monthly dividers through each ring or strip. Defaults to TRUE.
Set FALSE to omit the monthly divisions and retain the seasonal axis.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>sort.by</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Optional ordering by catalogue magnitude (<code>"mag"</code>), first R-only
sample (<code>"rise"</code>) or first S-only sample (<code>"set"</code>) on the stored
cycle. This is not sorting by the dated heliacal event. Missing classes are
placed last; omission retains input order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>pal</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Five colours in the order RS (rise and set), R (rise only), S (set only),
V (curtailed passage) and I (arising and lying hidden). The default uses five colours from the plot style. Monochrome adds textures to distinguish the classes. Supply all five even when only some
seasons occur.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>...</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Additional arguments to be passed to <em>plot</em>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>layout</code></th><td><code>c(&quot;auto&quot;, &quot;linear&quot;, &quot;circular&quot;)</code></td><td><p><code>"auto"</code> and <code>"circular"</code> draw a single ring or concentric rings
in input (or requested sort) order from the outside inward. Leaders connect the layer identifiers
to their rings. Select <code>"linear"</code> for strips. Supply this argument by name.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>style</code></th><td><code>&quot;publication-colour&quot;</code></td><td><p>Analytical display style, either <code>"publication-colour"</code> (default) or
<code>"publication-mono"</code>. Monochrome uses grayscale and preserves line styles.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Draws on the active graphics device and returns NULL invisibly.
</p><h5>Seasonal axis and comparison</h5><p>The axis is a 365-sample synthetic solar-longitude cycle anchored at December
solstice. Equinoxes and solstices mark quarter-cycle positions. The monthly
dividers mark twelve equal intervals of 30 degrees in solar longitude,
beginning at December solstice. For calendar dates use the underlying result's
<code>metadata$events$date.julian</code>, as described in <code>star.phases</code>.
</p><p>Objects may represent different stars, epochs, sites or model assumptions.
Shared star, epoch and site appear once. Different epochs of the same star label individual rings or rows. Mixed comparisons identify both star and year. Hold the site,
extinction and other inputs fixed for a controlled epoch comparison, or
state their differences in the figure caption. Names on the supplied list can
override the displayed star names. The legend contains only the union of
season classes present in the plotted objects.
</p><p>Event annotations use transitions between adjacent samples, including the last
and first samples of the cycle. A season continuing through December solstice
has no event at that boundary. Entry into and exit from I mark acronycal
setting and heliacal rising; entry into and exit from V mark acronycal rising
and heliacal setting. Constant classifications have no transition labels.
A single ring labels each event by name on two lines just outside the rim.
Its short leader meets the ring at the event's model day. A single ring shows the star, epoch and site in its centre
and labels the solstices and equinoxes outside its rim. Both layouts mark the event's model day,
the last sample before entry into I or V, or the first after exit.
The linear seasonal scale sits immediately below the lowest strip. Each quarter
label aligns with its solstice or equinox across every row. Rising-event labels
sit close above a single strip and setting-event labels close below it, leaving
room for the seasonal scale where needed. Both layouts use the same
sequence and colours; the circular layout makes the cycle boundary explicit.
Labels wrap and shrink to fit; crowded comparisons need a larger device.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/plotting.R`. [Full function help](help/plot.skyscapeR.starphases.html) · [Stellar visibility](stellar-phases.html#sec-stellar) · [Stellar positions and seasonal visibility outline](contents-plan.html#plan-stars) · [Comparing seasons](stellar-phases.html#phase-comparisons) · [The heliacal rising of the Pleiades](vignette-guide.html#workflow-the-heliacal-rising-of-the-pleiades) · [Compare stellar seasons](vignette-guide.html#workflow-compare-stellar-seasons)

### `star()` {#fn-star}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-star)

```{=html}
<p>A historical comparison requires a stellar coordinate for the epoch under study. The
function resolves a Western common name through star.names or accepts a catalogue
identifier and checks it against Swiss Ephemeris. It evaluates equatorial coordinates at
noon UT on 1 January of each supplied astronomical year in the Gregorian calendar. The
magnitude is a catalogue value. These outputs can feed horizon transformations or
visibility estimates, which additionally require observer and atmosphere information.
</p>
<p>The Swiss Ephemeris manual documents fixed-star positions and catalogue magnitudes.
</p>
```
