### `star.phases()` {#fn-star-phases}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-star-phases)

```{=html}
<p>Seasonal visibility depends on solar depression, stellar altitude, apparent magnitude
and atmospheric extinction as well as terrain. The model holds the star's position fixed
for the chosen year and samples a 365-day solar cycle with uniformly spaced ecliptic
longitudes. It requires a star-Sun altitude separation of 2.1 times the catalogue
magnitude plus 10 degrees, and compares extinction-adjusted magnitude with the limiting
magnitude. A positive-duration overlap of visibility conditions determines the daily
code. The stellar altitude trend within a visible interval below alt.rs determines
rising or setting. Terrain reappearance of a descending star therefore contributes
a setting phase. Disjoint runs are reported as separate seasons on the circular
model year, including runs spanning the December-solstice reference.
</p>
<p>Both constant and varying horizons are evaluated on all 365 model days. A horizon
object supplies the coordinates and piecewise-linear horizon. The profile must
cover all bearings and close at north. Use alt.hor only with coordinate input.
A fixed-coordinate stellar track is shared across model days. The terrain search
uses the same corners, azimuth reversals, interior extrema and 0.01-second root
tolerance as <code>riseset</code>, collecting all crossings during the model day.
Visible windows can lie wholly between minute samples. A touch without clearance
contributes no visible duration. Source terrain resolution and numerical tolerances
limit the shortest resolvable window.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Crumey, A. (2014). Human contrast threshold and astronomical
visibility. MNRAS 442, 2600-2619. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1093/mnras/stu992")}.
</p>
<p>Purrington, R. D. (1988). Heliacal Rising and Setting: Quantitative Aspects. Journal for the History of Astronomy 19, S72-S84. <a href="https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1988JHAS...19...72P">https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1988JHAS...19...72P</a>.
</p>
<p>Schaefer, B. E. (1986). Atmospheric Extinction Effects on Stellar Alignments. Journal for the History of Astronomy 17, S32-S42. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182868601701003")}.
</p>
<p>Schaefer, B. E. (1993). Astronomy and the Limits of Vision. Vistas in Astronomy 36, 311-361. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/0083-6656(93)90113-X")}.
</p>
<p>Schaefer, B. E. (1987). Heliacal Rise Phenomena. Journal for the History of Astronomy 18, S19-S33. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182868701801103")}.
</p>
<p>Brady, B. (2015). Star Phases: the Naked-eye Astronomy of the Old Kingdom Pyramid Texts. In F. Silva and N. Campion (eds), Skyscapes: The Role and Importance of the Sky in Archaeology. Oxbow Books, pp. 76-86.
</p>
<p>Krisciunas, K. and Schaefer, B. E. (1991). A model of the brightness
of moonlight. PASP 103, 1033-1039 (equation 14 for extinction airmass).
\Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1086/132921")}.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Track clearance, seasonal visibility and the representative Julian date are different outputs. Month and phase labels organise the cycle; deciding whether a star could be detected requires a time interval above the actual skyline.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>star</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Either the star name or a <em>skyscapeR.star</em> object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>The year of interest. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Location, either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> or a vector
containing the latitude, longitude and elevation of location, in this order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt.hor</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>The altitude of the horizon to consider.
Defaults to zero degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt.rs</code></th><td><code>10</code></td><td><p>The maximum altitude of a star's first or last
visibility for it to still be considered to be as rising or setting.
Defaults to ten degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>solar.alt</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Solar altitude threshold in degrees. NULL uses
-6 for a horizon, or alt.hor - 6 for coordinate input.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>k</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.vars()$k</code></td><td><p>Visual extinction in magnitudes per airmass (Schaefer 1986, p. S33). The package adopts 0.2 as a clear-sky baseline. Extinction varies with site and atmospheric conditions (Schaefer 1986, 1993). Defaults to the session value from skyscapeR.vars().</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>limit</code></th><td><code>6</code></td><td><p>The maximum magnitude of a star that can be
visible with the naked eye. Defaults to 6.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Logical. Apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Atmospheric pressure in mbar. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>res</code></th><td><code>1/24/6</code></td><td><p>Spacing of solar altitude samples in days, greater than zero and at
most one. Default 1/144 day (ten minutes). Terrain crossings are refined separately.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.starphases list. The data table gives each model day and its phase code: I for invisible, V for visible without a classified rise or set, R for rising, S for setting and RS for both. Metadata include the star, year, observer coordinates, phase type, season and event tables, refraction setting and solar altitude threshold. For a named horizon, <code>metadata$site.name</code> retains the site label for comparisons. The logical <code>metadata$horizon</code> records whether a horizon object was supplied. The separate <code>metadata$horizon.status</code> reports <code>"always above"</code>, <code>"always below"</code> or <code>"crosses"</code> relative to the supplied skyline. Event rows include solar.longitude in degrees on the synthetic cycle. The date.julian column gives the representative local Julian calendar date at the supplied longitude. Pass this date to <code>riseset</code> with <code>calendar = "J"</code> to time the skyline crossing. For a dawn sketch, advance from that crossing until the star clears the terrain while the sky is still dark enough. The phase date alone does not specify a visible instant.
</p><h5>Extinction and model scope</h5><p>The implementation uses Rozenberg's airmass approximation,
<i>X(h)=1/(\sin h+0.025\exp(-11\sin h))</i>, multiplying it by <code>k</code>
and adding the result to the fixed catalogue magnitude. Here <code>h</code> is the
stellar altitude selected by <code>refraction</code>, above the astronomical
horizontal. This is distinct from the height above a ridge. The star-Sun
altitude-separation rule uses the catalogue magnitude before extinction.
</p><p>The model does not calculate scattered moonlight, artificial light pollution,
weather, an observer's adaptation history, or variable-star light curves.
The same separation threshold is used at all relative azimuths. It is therefore
a screening model for seasonal opportunities, not a probability of detection.
Supplying an integrated cluster entry such as M45 treats its total magnitude as
one target; cluster size, surface brightness and resolution into individual
stars do not enter this calculation. It does not predict when each Pleiad is
individually visible.
</p><p>Horizon status is determined from positive-duration clearance intervals along
the same stellar track used for the phase calculation, with the supplied
skyline and refraction setting. The same calculation applies in both
hemispheres. A track with no clearance returns an ordinary all-I result,
rather than raising an error. An always-clear track still undergoes the
extinction and solar-darkness tests; never setting does not imply visibility.
A star that never sets below a level horizontal can cross a raised ridge.
Isolated tangencies do not count as intervals of clearance or obstruction.
Numerical resolution and the supplied terrain profile limit this status.
</p><p>The separate metadata$horizon.status field is "always above", "always below"
or "crosses", relative to the supplied skyline. Phase codes R and S describe
the rising or descending part of a visible track below alt.rs; they do not
require a physical skyline crossing that day. An always-clear star may thus
have seasonal R/S codes. The type "circumpolar" is retained for an all-V
result only when the track is always above the skyline; other all-V results
are labelled "visible throughout cycle". Use horizon.status, not type, to
distinguish clearance from seasonal visibility.
</p><h5>Dates and a subsequent sky sketch</h5><p>Events follow adjacent-sample transitions around the closed cycle, including
the December-solstice boundary. Entering and leaving I mark acronycal setting
and heliacal rising; entering and leaving V mark acronycal rising and heliacal
setting. A season continuing across the boundary creates no event there.
Constant phase sequences have no transition events.
</p><p>The 365 model samples are equally spaced in solar longitude, not in elapsed
civil time. Printed seasonal labels are anchored to the December solstice.
<code>metadata$events$date.julian</code> instead solves for the event solar longitude
in the requested year and converts it to a local mean-solar Julian-calendar
date using longitude. It is a representative date, not an exact detection
instant, and can differ from the synthetic <code>day</code> label.
</p><p>Pass the representative date to <code>riseset</code> with
<code>calendar = "J"</code> and an explicit timezone. With UTC or a fixed offset,
inspect neighbouring dates when local mean-solar and civil days differ.
The returned rise is a skyline crossing. Follow it by a short time sequence
with <code>sketchSky</code> and <code>skyStep</code> to inspect terrain
clearance and the changing brightness of the local sky.
</p><p>A supplied <code>skyscapeR.star</code> is used as given. Recompute it for the requested
year; the phase function does not update an existing object's coordinates.
</p><h5>How precise is a heliacal-rising date?</h5><p>In 69 of 70 individual comparisons, the estimated first morning of visibility was within a week of the predicted heliacal-rising date.
</p><h5>Reproducing a saved result</h5><p>Metadata retain the resolved star, year, observer coordinates, extinction,
atmospheric settings and solar-altitude threshold, together with <code>limit</code>,
<code>alt.rs</code>, <code>res</code> and <code>alt.hor</code>. The latter is NA when a terrain
profile replaces the constant horizon. <code>metadata$horizon.profile</code> contains
the numerical <code>az</code>/<code>alt</code> table used, or NULL for a constant horizon.
Landscape images and DEMs are not copied into the result. Existing logical
<code>horizon</code> and <code>skyline</code> fields are retained.
</p><p><code>metadata$provenance$packages</code> records the loaded skyscapeR and swephR
versions; an unavailable version is NA, for example when sourcing functions
outside a package namespace. Version strings do not uniquely identify
development builds. Retain the original script, code revision and ephemeris
files as well: the saved metadata do not identify or archive those files.
Earlier saved results do not acquire these fields automatically.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/stars.R`. ## Sky brightness and visualisation {#group-light}

Separate the ephemeris and local geometry, the radiance model, and the mapping of radiance to a display. The natural and publication styles answer different questions about a reconstruction.

### `importConstellations()` {#fn-importconstellations}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-importconstellations)

```{=html}
<p>Each non-comment line contains a unique figure identifier, the number
of segments, then two Hipparcos numbers per segment. Endpoints describe
separate pairs, not one continuous polygon. Blank lines and comments beginning
with a hash are ignored. Non-negative segment counts and positive integer HIP identifiers are validated.
Zero-segment records are retained with an empty HIP field and skipped when drawn.
Repeated endpoints represent a single-star figure, drawn as a small ring.
This supports Stellarium's legacy constellationship.fab format, not the JSON
sky-culture format introduced in Stellarium 25.1. Only lines are imported,
not artwork, labels, boundaries or star positions. Endpoint stars must be in
skyscapeR's stellar catalogue; unavailable stars produce warnings when drawn.
The import does not modify the bundled catalogue or register global names.
Save the returned object with saveRDS(), or load the file in each script.
Respect the source sky culture's attribution and redistribution terms.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Stellarium User Guide, Adding Sky Cultures (legacy editions) and
Sky Cultures (current editions): <a href="https://stellarium.org/guide/">https://stellarium.org/guide/</a>.
Legacy example: <a href="https://github.com/Stellarium/stellarium/blob/v0.22.2/skycultures/western/constellationship.fab">https://github.com/Stellarium/stellarium/blob/v0.22.2/skycultures/western/constellationship.fab</a>.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A drawn figure expresses a chosen connection between catalogue stars. Endpoints, projection and cultural attribution must be documented separately from any claim that the figure was visible together at a particular instant.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>file</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Path to a Stellarium legacy constellationship.fab text file.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>set</code></th><td><code>&quot;custom&quot;</code></td><td><p>Label for this collection, default "custom".</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A data frame with the same columns as <code>constellations</code>, accepted by
the <code>display$constellations</code> setting of <code>sketchSky</code> or the
<code>constellations</code> argument of <code>planisphere</code>. Subset rows to select individual figures.
</p>
```

### `planisphere()` {#fn-planisphere}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-planisphere)

```{=html}
<p>The default star layer draws individual Pleiades members and omits integrated clusters and other nonstellar entries. The full catalogue remains available for target searches and phase calculations.
</p>
<p>The chart compares the accessible part of the celestial sphere with a catalogue sky at
the chosen year. Catalogue stars are filtered by magnitude and by the implemented
declinations that rise above a level geometric horizon. Northern latitudes use
the north celestial pole; southern latitudes use the south celestial pole.
Polar distance sets radius, and right ascension sets angle with opposite
handedness for the two poles. Magnitude controls symbol size, and hour labels
are placed every three hours. The optional ecliptic uses daily solar positions over a
year, using geocentric coordinates without atmospheric refraction. The plot is
not an instantaneous view
through a site's measured horizon. The Milky Way uses the same diffuse-light tracing as sketchSky(), with dark cutouts and two brighter tiers referenced to the whole-band mean. Source: NASA/Goddard SVS and ESA/Gaia/DPAC, Deep Star Maps 2020. It is a fixed sky map rotated to the requested epoch with Swiss Ephemeris precession and nutation. Its width is illustrative. It does not predict visibility or reconstruct the Galaxy’s internal evolution.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio (2020).
Deep Star Maps 2020. <a href="https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4851/">https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4851/</a>.
</p>
<p>Astrodienst. Swiss Ephemeris programmer's manual.
<a href="https://www.astro.com/swisseph/swephprg.htm">https://www.astro.com/swisseph/swephprg.htm</a>.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A drawn figure expresses a chosen connection between catalogue stars. Endpoints, projection and cultural attribution must be documented separately from any claim that the figure was visible together at a particular instant.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>The epoch (year) for which the planisphere is calculated. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>lat</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Observer latitude in degrees north, between -90 and 90.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>max.mag</code></th><td><code>6</code></td><td><p>Faintest catalogue magnitude drawn as a star symbol (default 6). This does not filter constellation line endpoints.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.ecliptic</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Whether to display the ecliptic (TRUE or FALSE).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col.ecliptic</code></th><td><code>&quot;#A9542E&quot;</code></td><td><p>Colour of the ecliptic line (default ochre).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.equator</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Whether to display the celestial equator (TRUE or FALSE).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col.equator</code></th><td><code>&quot;#597575&quot;</code></td><td><p>Colour of the celestial equator (default muted grey-green).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>star.col</code></th><td><code>&quot;#23383A&quot;</code></td><td><p>Colour of the star symbols (default dark grey-green).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>epoch</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Earlier argument name for <code>year</code>, retained for existing scripts.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.milky.way</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Draw the Milky Way behind the stars (default TRUE). Set to FALSE for a chart without the band.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.galactic.equator</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>Draw the Galactic equator as a dash-dot line. Default FALSE.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>constellations</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Optional constellation selection: a bundled set such as
<code>"modern"</code>, <code>"chinese"</code> or <code>"chinese_mansions"</code>, figure names
or identifiers, or a table from <code>importConstellations</code>.
The default <code>NULL</code> draws no constellation lines.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col.constellations</code></th><td><code>&quot;#638582&quot;</code></td><td><p>Colour of the constellation lines (default muted teal).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.legend</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Show chart pole, latitude, epoch, magnitude limit and the enabled layer key.
FALSE centres the bare chart, keeping its data and right-ascension ticks.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>style</code></th><td><code>&quot;publication-colour&quot;</code></td><td><p>Analytical display style, either <code>"publication-colour"</code> (default) or
<code>"publication-mono"</code>. Monochrome uses grayscale and preserves line styles.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Draws the polar chart on the active graphics device and invisibly returns the saved xpd, mar and pty graphics settings.
</p><h5>Constellation patterns</h5><p>Constellation segments follow the shorter great-circle arc between catalogue
endpoints at the requested epoch. They use the same polar projection as the
stars and are clipped to the chart's accessible sky. Faint endpoints remain
available for line drawing even when no star symbol is shown. Missing catalogue
endpoints generate a warning and their segments are omitted. These are line
figures; repeated endpoints mark single-star figures with small rings. They
are not constellation boundaries or lunar-mansion sectors. See
<code>constellations</code> for sources, licences and historical limitations.
</p><h5>Projection and visibility limits</h5><p>This is a polar azimuthal equidistant chart. For latitude at or above zero,
radius is 90 minus declination and right ascension increases clockwise from
the top. For negative latitude, radius is 90 plus declination and right
ascension increases anticlockwise. The chart radius is 180 minus absolute
latitude; a non-round cutoff is retained exactly. All layers use this same
projection. At the equator the north-polar convention is used.
</p><p>Stars are included when their upper culmination is strictly above a level
geometric horizon; stars that only touch it are excluded. This is potential
annual access to that part of the sky, not visibility at any particular time.
There is no date/time of night, local terrain, atmospheric extinction,
moonlight or twilight detection model. Magnitudes are fixed catalogue values,
and point size is a graphical brightness indicator. For a particular site and
instant use <code>sketchSky</code> with a georeferenced horizon.
</p>
```

</details>

### `sketchSky()` {#fn-sketchsky}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-sketchsky)

```{=html}
<p>The function computes an object without drawing. Use
<code>plot(hor, sky = sky, xrange = ..., yrange = ...)</code> to choose the sector.
Replotting the object changes framing without recalculating the instant. Use
<code>skyStep</code> to recalculate at another time. Astronomical calculations
require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch; see
<code>skyscapeR-package</code> for installation.
</p>
```

```{=html}
</p>
<p>Schaefer, B. E. (1993). Astronomy and the Limits of Vision.
Vistas in Astronomy 36, 311-361. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/0083-6656(93)90113-X")}.
</p>
<p>Lee, R. L., Jr. (1994). Twilight and daytime colors of the clear sky.
Applied Optics 33, 4629-4638. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1364/AO.33.004629")}.

Venus. Applied Optics 54, B194-B203. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1364/AO.54.00B194")}.
</p>

visibility. MNRAS 442, 2600-2619. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1093/mnras/stu992")}.
</p>
<p>NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio
(2020). Deep Star Maps 2020. <a href="https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4851/">https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4851/</a>.
</p>

```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** For photometric claims work with the linear component matrices and pixel area. Changing the field of view or display mapping can change screen intensity even when integrated source flux is conserved.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <code>skyscapeR.horizon</code> with finite latitude, longitude and observer
elevation in metres in <code>metadata$georef</code>. The numerical profile supplies the
foreground when plotted. A panorama image is optional.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>jd</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>One finite UT Julian day. Supply exactly one of <code>jd</code> and <code>time</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>time</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>A civil timestamp accepted by <code>time2jd</code>, or a POSIXt instant.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Civil timezone and calendar for character <code>time</code>, as
in <code>time2jd</code>. Defaults are the session settings. A POSIXt value already
identifies an instant; these arguments do not reinterpret it. Use UTC or a fixed
offset for ancient civil dates.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Civil timezone and calendar for character <code>time</code>, as
in <code>time2jd</code>. Defaults are the session settings. A POSIXt value already
identifies an instant; these arguments do not reinterpret it. Use UTC or a fixed
offset for ancient civil dates.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>display</code></th><td><code>list()</code></td><td><p>A named list of logical switches: <code>sun</code>, <code>moon</code>,
<code>planets</code>, <code>stars</code>, <code>constellation.lines</code>, <code>milky.way</code>,
<code>galactic.equator</code>, <code>ecliptic</code>, <code>equator</code>, <code>poles</code> and
<code>zenith</code>. Sun, Moon and stars default to TRUE; other switches default to
FALSE, except that the Milky Way follows <code>stars</code> unless explicitly set.
The additional <code>constellations</code> entry accepts names or an imported data
frame, rather than a logical value. See Constellations below. A named logical
vector is sufficient when supplying only switches.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>style</code></th><td><code>c(&quot;natural&quot;, &quot;publication-colour&quot;, &quot;publication-mono&quot;)</code></td><td><p>One of <code>"natural"</code>, <code>"publication-colour"</code> or
<code>"publication-mono"</code>. Publication styles have a white background and dark
guides. Colour uses muted stellar and planetary colours and a warm solar disc;
mono uses black and white. Neither publication style predicts visibility.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>max.mag</code></th><td><code>6</code></td><td><p>Finite catalogue magnitude cutoff, default 6. Applied before
extinction to star symbols and the integrated magnitudes of supported clusters.
It does not limit constellation endpoints, the Sun, Moon or planets. Raising
the cutoff includes additional stars only where the catalogue supplies them.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>k</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.vars()$k</code></td><td><p>Non-negative visual extinction coefficient in magnitudes per airmass
for natural style. Defaults to <code>skyscapeR.vars()$k</code>, initially 0.2.
This clear-sky baseline is an assumption, not an estimate of the site's weather.
Zero removes extinction and the modelled lunar scattering. Publication styles
do not apply extinction to symbols.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>An object of classes <code>skyscapeR.sketch</code> and <code>skyscapeR.sky</code>.
It stores <code>jd</code>, <code>loc</code>, <code>style</code>, <code>display</code>, <code>settings</code>
(calendar, magnitude cutoff and extinction), and <code>atmosphere</code>.
<code>stars</code> and <code>coords</code> contain azimuth, altitude and symbol size;
<code>star.opacity</code> retains an earlier symbol-opacity diagnostic; natural
sketches draw from <code>light.budget</code>. <code>bodies</code>, <code>diameters</code>,
<code>planet.size</code> and <code>lunar</code> describe selected Solar System bodies.
<code>clusters</code> holds supported cluster footprints and opacity when applicable;
<code>guides</code>, <code>light</code>, <code>background</code> and twilight fields support drawing.
Components can be empty when a layer is disabled. No image file is written.
</p><h5>Reading a natural sketch</h5><p>The sky is calculated for the specified instant. Stars, clusters, planets and
the Moon contribute light on a common visual (V-band) magnitude scale.
Diffuse Milky Way light and atmospheric background are measured per unit
sky area. Their light is added before brightness is compressed for display.
To inspect the values underlying a view, use <code>skyRadiance</code>.
</p><p>Stars remain unresolved as the field is enlarged. Mercury, Venus, Mars,
Jupiter, Saturn and the Moon use apparent disc sizes and illuminated
fractions from Swiss Ephemeris. A close view can therefore show the phase
of Venus. Star colours follow catalogue spectral classes; the diffuse band
has a neutral tint. Colour and projection influence the screen appearance.
Publication styles use magnitude-scaled star and planet symbols on white.
</p><p>Azimuth increases clockwise from true north. Refraction, pressure and
temperature come from <code>skyscapeR.vars</code> when the sky is calculated.
The Sun and Moon switches control their contributions to sky illumination as
well as their discs. Use <code>display = list(moon = FALSE)</code> for a moonless
comparison. The terrain masks the drawn sky; a local ridge hiding the Moon
can still leave scattered moonlight in the sky.
</p><h5>Constellations</h5><p>Use <code>display = list(constellations = "Orion")</code> to select and enable line
figures. <code>"modern"</code> selects all 88 Western figures, <code>"chinese"</code> the
full Chinese set, and <code>"chinese_mansions"</code> the 28 lunar-mansion figures.
Names and abbreviations are case-sensitive; for example <code>c("Ori", "Tau")</code>.
Alternatively, supply a data frame from <code>importConstellations</code>.
See <code>constellations</code> for sources and identifiers.
</p><p>Supplying a selection enables lines unless <code>constellation.lines = FALSE</code>
is also supplied. Setting <code>constellation.lines = TRUE</code> without a selection
uses modern figures. Endpoint coordinates are calculated independently of the
star-symbol magnitude cut. Lines therefore remain when their stars are faint,
extincted, or switched off. A single-star figure is drawn as a ring. Normal
plot clipping and the horizon foreground still apply. These are reference
figures; their visibility is not an observing prediction.
</p><h5>Twilight and extinction</h5><p>At twilight the sky brightens differently towards and away from the Sun.
Zenith brightness uses the Paranal V-band observations of Patat et al.
(2006) at solar depressions of 5 to 15 degrees. Sacramento Peak measurements
supply earlier twilight levels and the directional variation (Koomen et al.
1952). These clear-sky estimates depend on site conditions. Moonlight uses
the scattering model of Krisciunas and Schaefer (1991), with its dependence
on lunar phase, altitude and angular separation.
</p><p>Direct light fades towards the horizon as its path through the atmosphere
lengthens. The coefficient <code>k</code> sets the loss per airmass. The model
uses Rozenberg's airmass approximation (Krisciunas and Schaefer 1991);
uncertainty is greatest close to the skyline. The twilight colours are
illustrative (Lee 1994, 2015).
</p><h5>Milky Way and clusters</h5><p>The Milky Way is traced from the diffuse light in Deep Star Maps 2020.
Within the smoothed envelope, retained dark patches have at least 10 percent
local contrast; two bright tiers begin at 1.10 and 1.75 times the mean band
tone after the dark patches are excluded. Retained patches cover at least
10 square degrees. Natural sketches anchor the mean surface brightness
of a four-degree field in Carina to 20.7 V magnitudes per square arcsecond
(van der Kruit 2024). Brightness elsewhere is approximate. Atmospheric
extinction can make the band difficult to follow down to its calculated
horizon crossing. The Galactic equator is an optional geometric guide.
</p><p>A supported cluster contributes its catalogue light across its angular
extent. Light already assigned to plotted stars within that footprint is
subtracted before the remaining glow is drawn. This accounts for projected
overlap; it does not establish membership. Integrated cluster magnitude
alone is insufficient to predict first detection (Crumey 2014).
</p><h5>Using a sketch with a stellar phase date</h5><p>In 69 of 70 individual comparisons, the estimated first morning of visibility was within a week of the predicted heliacal-rising date.
</p><p>Use <code>riseset</code> to locate the skyline crossing on each morning,
then <code>skyStep</code> to follow the star as it climbs through a
brightening sky. A plotted pixel does not establish naked-eye visibility.
A quantitative test needs a point-source threshold and an assumed observer
limit (Crumey 2014). See also <code>star.phases</code>.
Record site, horizon, epoch, calendar, timezone, extinction
and display switches when reporting a reconstruction.
</p>
```

</details>

### `skyRadiance()` {#fn-skyradiance}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-skyradiance)

```{=html}
<p>Direct light includes stars, residual cluster light, planetary discs
and the illuminated lunar disc. The Milky Way uses the accepted tracing and
a provisional Carina surface-brightness calibration. Stars remain unresolved
as the view is enlarged. See <code>sketchSky</code> for sources, assumptions
and interpretation.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** For photometric claims work with the linear component matrices and pixel area. Changing the field of view or display mapping can change screen intensity even when integrated source flux is conserved.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>sky</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A natural sketch from <code>sketchSky</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>xrange</code></th><td><code>c(0, 360)</code></td><td><p>Increasing true azimuth limits in degrees. A sector may cross
north, for example c(340,380).</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>yrange</code></th><td><code>c(0, 90)</code></td><td><p>Increasing altitude limits within -90 to 90 degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>size</code></th><td><code>c(720, 180)</code></td><td><p>Positive integer column and row counts, up to 1600 by 1000.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A list containing azimuth and altitude pixel centres, total radiance,
direct light (stars, residual cluster light, planets and lunar disc), and
Milky Way radiance. Matrices are in magnitude-zero flux units per square
degree, ordered from high to low altitude and increasing azimuth. Multiply
by area (square degrees per pixel by row) and sum to obtain flux. The
difference between total and the two source matrices is the atmospheric
background. The Sun contributes to the background; its disc is a plot overlay.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/light-budget.R`. [Full function help](help/skyRadiance.html) · [Sky reconstruction](sky-rendering.html#sec-sketch) · [Sky brightness and visualisation outline](contents-plan.html#plan-light) · [Display styles, capture and stepping time](sky-rendering.html#sky-step-capture)

### `skyStep()` {#fn-skystep}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-skystep)

```{=html}
<p>Add the signed increment in minutes divided by 1440 to the saved Julian date. A native sketch is recalculated locally using the saved display selection, style, extinction and magnitude limit, and the current session atmosphere. A Stellarium capture is repeated using its saved external capture settings. The function plots the new view and invisibly returns its sky object. Assign that return value to continue the sequence from the new instant. The remote connection is needed only for the capture branch.</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Preserve the sky object or captured image and the settings of the system that produced it. Stepping through several instants is informative near a terrain crossing; a screen capture alone carries no per-pixel naked-eye detection threshold.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Site horizon with latitude, longitude and elevation in metres.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>sky</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A background returned by sketchSky(), stellariumSky() or skyStep().</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>minutes</code></th><td><code>1</code></td><td><p>Signed elapsed minutes from the captured instant. Fractions are allowed.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>...</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Arguments passed to plot(hor, sky=...), such as xrange.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>stellariumSky() returns a skyscapeR.sky object with the native raster, PNG path, Julian day, observer location and capture settings. skyStep() invisibly returns the updated sky of the same kind.
</p><h5>Reproducibility and stepping</h5><p>A Stellarium capture reflects the installed Stellarium version, its catalogues,
selected sky culture and current settings for switches not explicitly supplied.
It is an external rendered image, not the package's twilight or extinction
model. Record those settings when comparing it with <code>sketchSky</code>.
The external application and a working local Remote Control connection are
required for every new capture, but not for replotting a saved raster.
</p><h5>Atmospheric settings when using skyStep</h5><p>For a sketch, <code>skyStep</code> retains calendar, <code>max.mag</code>, <code>k</code>, style
and display selections. Refraction, pressure and temperature are read again
from <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>; the previous object's atmosphere is not
restored automatically. Changing these session settings between the original
sketch and a step changes the atmosphere as well as the time. Keep them fixed
for a time-only comparison, including when resuming a saved sketch in another
R session. This behaviour is intentional. Stellarium captures instead use
the external application's atmospheric settings.
Each call draws immediately and returns the new object invisibly. Save it with
<code>sky &lt;- skyStep(hor, sky, minutes = 10)</code> before taking the next step.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/skybox.R`. ### `stellariumSky()` {#fn-stellariumsky}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-stellariumsky)

```{=html}
<p>Enable Remote Control under Configuration &gt; Plugins in Stellarium Desktop, select Load at startup and restart if needed. Enable the server in the plugin settings. Use the local server without a password and install the R packages httr2 and png. Close dialogs and use a normal rectangular viewport. Point screenshot.dir at the directory configured in Stellarium.
</p>
<p>The script freezes time and takes one full-sphere Cylinder Fill screenshot. The centre is south, the seam is north, and the horizon is halfway up. Choose width for more pixels per degree. R keeps the native pixels for each plotted sector. For a 30-degree sector a width of 8192 supplies about 683 source pixels. The physical plot size and graphics device determine the displayed resolution. If the script times out, check the screenshot path and that your Stellarium version offers Cylinder Fill.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Preserve the sky object or captured image and the settings of the system that produced it. Stepping through several instants is informative near a terrain crossing; a screen capture alone carries no per-pixel naked-eye detection threshold.

Supply either jd or time.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>screenshot.dir</code></th><td><code>getOption(&quot;skyscapeR.screenshot.dir&quot;, &quot;~/Pictures/Stellarium&quot;)</code></td><td><p>Existing local directory where Stellarium writes screenshots.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>port</code></th><td><code>8090L</code></td><td><p>Local Remote Control server port.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timeout</code></th><td><code>60</code></td><td><p>Maximum wait for the capture in seconds.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>time</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>A date and clock time such as "2026/12/21 16:00", or a POSIXct or POSIXlt instant.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>timezone</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>For character time, a zone name or fixed UTC offset as in time2jd(). Defaults to the package setting.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>calendar</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>For character time, the Gregorian or Julian calendar as in time2jd(). Defaults to the package setting.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>display</code></th><td><code>c(landscape = FALSE, fog = FALSE)</code></td><td><p>Named logical switches: atmosphere, landscape, fog, cardinals, compass.marks (numbered horizon bearings), azimuthal.grid, equatorial.grid, constellation.lines, constellation.labels (names) and constellation.art. Use galactic.equator to toggle the Galactic equator independently of the equatorial grid. ## Uncertainty and orientation distributions {#group-density}

Record the density family, sampling interval, cutoff, coordinate transformation and any unit-area normalisation. Interpolating an SPD onto a finer grid does not improve a bearing measurement.

### `az.pdf()` {#fn-az-pdf}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-az-pdf)

```{=html}
<p>A field bearing defines a centre and an angular uncertainty. Model the uncertainty as a
normal density with the supplied standard deviation, or as a uniform density over the
centre plus or minus the supplied half-width. A scalar uncertainty is reused for each
measurement. The function samples from -90 to 450 degrees, folds the overlapping tails
across north and retains density values at or above the cutoff. Use a spacing compatible
with a full turn on the grid. The input measurements remain separate and truncated tails
are not renormalised. The supported families are normal and uniform.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Silva, F (2020) A probabilistic framework and significance test for the analysis of structural orientations
in skyscape archaeology <em>Journal of Archaeological Science</em> 118, 105138. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jas.2020.105138")}
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A reported uncertainty enters differently as the standard deviation of a normal density and as the half-width of a uniform density. Record which interpretation the measurement supports before combining sites.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>True bearings in degrees clockwise from north, one per observation.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>unc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Angular uncertainty in degrees, one value shared across observations or one per azimuth. For a normal distribution this is the standard deviation. For a uniform distribution it is the half-width on either side of the measurement.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>pdf</code></th><td><code>&quot;normal&quot;</code></td><td><p>Uncertainty distribution. Choose <code>"normal"</code> (default) or <code>"uniform"</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Optional labels in the same order as the measurements.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.res</code></th><td><code>0.01</code></td><td><p>Spacing of the output bearing grid in degrees. Default 0.01.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.cutoff</code></th><td><code>1e-05</code></td><td><p>Minimum density retained on the output grid. Default <code>1e-5</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>T</code></td><td><p>Logical. Display progress or informational messages. Default <code>TRUE</code>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.pdf list. The data component contains one data frame per measurement, in input order, with azimuth x in degrees and density y. The metadata record the measurements, names, uncertainties, distribution type and numerical settings.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/statistics.R`. ### `coordtrans()` {#fn-coordtrans}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-coordtrans)

```{=html}
<p>A sightline has a distribution of possible bearings, and each bearing samples a
potentially different part of the horizon. For every sampled bearing the function
interpolates horizon altitude and uncertainty, maps an altitude range to declination and
approximates the conditional declination distribution by a Gaussian. It weights that
distribution by the azimuth density and integrates the product by the trapezoidal rule.
A shared horizon can serve several observations, or a supplied list can represent their
individual sites.
</p>
<p>Density values are calculated at declination spacing <code>.res</code>, then
linearly interpolated onto a grid with spacing <code>.output.res</code>. The upper
calculation bound is evaluated explicitly if the step does not land on it,
avoiding extrapolation at the tail. Linear interpolation preserves
nonnegative calculated densities and avoids cubic-spline overshoot.
Individual PDF outputs retain their existing area normalisation; SPD outputs
retain their existing unnormalised transformation behaviour. Coarse
calculation spacing can still miss narrow peaks; interpolation does not
replace a resolution-convergence check. Azimuth integration uses a separate
grid from -90 to 450 degrees with step <code>.prec</code>. For a distribution split across north, integration uses contiguous bearings around zero at the same spacing. The output grid starts
at the lower bound and ends at the last full step within the upper bound.
Refine the calculation grid to check that narrow features are resolved.
Set atmospheric refraction, pressure and temperature with <code>skyscapeR.vars</code> before transforming. The values used are recorded in the returned PDF or SPD.
All three spacings are stored in <code>metadata$param</code>.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Silva, F (2020) A probabilistic framework and significance test for the analysis of structural orientations
in skyscape archaeology <em>Journal of Archaeological Science</em> 118, 105138. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jas.2020.105138")}
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A transformed density inherits the latitude and skyline for its own bearing. Replacing it with a symmetric curve can erase an asymmetric or multimodal distribution created by the terrain.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>pdf</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <em>skyscapeR.pdf</em> object created with <code>az.pdf</code> or a <em>skyscapeR.spd</em> object created with <code>spd</code></p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A shared <code>skyscapeR.horizon</code> or, for individual azimuth PDFs, a list of horizons in measurement order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>xrange</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Array of values (min and max) for SPD when transforming a <em>skyscapeR.spd</em> object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.res</code></th><td><code>0.1</code></td><td><p>Spacing of the declination calculation grid, in degrees. Default 0.1.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.prec</code></th><td><code>0.1</code></td><td><p>Azimuth integration spacing, in degrees. Default 0.1.
Previously ignored; smaller values increase integration work. Must not exceed 540.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.output.res</code></th><td><code>0.01</code></td><td><p>Spacing of the returned declination grid, in degrees.
Default 0.01. Coarser spacing reduces output size. All spacings must be
positive finite scalars, and the returned grid must contain at least two points.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Logical. Display progress or informational messages. Default <code>TRUE</code>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A <code>skyscapeR.pdf</code> object for PDF input, or a <code>skyscapeR.spd</code>
object for SPD input. Both contain <code>metadata</code> and <code>data</code>. PDF data
are a list of data frames with declination <code>x</code> and density <code>y</code>;
SPD data are a single such data frame. Metadata include the coordinate type,
transformation settings, format version and descriptive source labels.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/statistics.R`. ### `dec.pdf()` {#fn-dec-pdf}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-dec-pdf)

```{=html}
<p>A declination estimate already incorporates the sightline geometry. This constructor
works directly in that coordinate. For each centre it evaluates a normal density with
the given standard deviation or a uniform density with the given half-width. A single
uncertainty is shared, or one can be supplied per observation. Save the original
uncertainty interpretation when comparing results from different surveys.
</p>
<p>Each grid is restricted to physical declinations and trimmed at .cutoff. The retained curve is not renormalised after truncation. Use <code>spd</code> to combine measurements.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Silva, F. (2020). A probabilistic framework and significance test for the analysis of structural orientations in skyscape archaeology. Journal of Archaeological Science 118, 105138. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jas.2020.105138")}.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A reported uncertainty enters differently as the standard deviation of a normal density and as the half-width of a uniform density. Record which interpretation the measurement supports before combining sites.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>dec</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Measured declinations in degrees, between -90 and 90 inclusive.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>unc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Positive uncertainties in degrees of declination. Supply one value or one per measurement. For normal densities this is the standard deviation. For uniform densities it is the half-width.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>pdf</code></th><td><code>&quot;normal&quot;</code></td><td><p>Distribution family, "normal" or "uniform", with the same abbreviations as <code>az.pdf</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>name</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Optional measurement labels in input order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.res</code></th><td><code>0.01</code></td><td><p>Grid spacing in degrees. Default 0.01.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.cutoff</code></th><td><code>1e-04</code></td><td><p>Minimum retained density height. Default 0.0001.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Logical. Report completion.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.pdf list with one x/y data frame per observation. Metadata record coord = "dec", the input measurements, family, uncertainties, labels and numerical settings.
</p>
```

</details>

### `hpdi()` {#fn-hpdi}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-hpdi)

```{=html}
<p>A distribution with several peaks can give several disjoint intervals. The mass
parameter applies to the selected regions together; the result describes concentration
of the supplied density rather than significance against a null model.
</p>
<p>Uses the existing discrete density-threshold method: sort sampled
densities, find the threshold reaching the requested fraction of their sum,
and include all points tied at that threshold. Consequently, the selected
mass can exceed the requested value. Densities need not sum to one.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Hyndman, R. J. (1996). Computing and Graphing Highest Density Regions. The American Statistician 50, 120-126. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1080/00031305.1996.10474359")}.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A summed curve depends on its inputs, grid and normalisation. Selecting a subset changes the archaeological population being summarised. A highest-density interval describes concentrated probability mass, with no null-model adjustment.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>x</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <em>skyscapeR.spd</em> or <em>skyscapeR.pdf</em> object,
or one data frame/list with numeric components <code>x</code> and <code>y</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>mass</code></th><td><code>0.954</code></td><td><p>Probability mass, greater than zero and at most one.
Default is 0.954.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>For a PDF object, a list of interval matrices, one per distribution,
even for a single distribution. For SPD or x/y input, one matrix.
Each matrix has columns <code>start</code> and <code>end</code>, with ordered endpoints
and one row per contiguous region, sorted by start.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/misc.R`. [Full function help](help/hpdi.html) · [Uncertainty and orientation distributions outline](contents-plan.html#plan-density) · [From a measured orientation to a declination distribution](orientation-densities.html#density-summary)

### `plot.skyscapeR.pdf()` {#fn-plot-skyscaper-pdf}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-plot-skyscaper-pdf)

```{=html}
<p>Individual curves reveal whether measurements overlap or have disjoint high-density
regions. In the stacked view, each selected density is scaled by its own peak for
display and its highest-density regions are shaded using hpdi. Heights across different
rows therefore do not measure relative probability mass. Use the linked panels for one
transformed observation to inspect how its source azimuth distribution and horizon
produce the declination distribution. Its annotation gives the measurement name
and the highest-density declination interval or intervals containing the requested
probability mass. Every disjoint component is listed in the HDR readout. Standalone curves have a fixed label column.
</p>
<p>With neither source input supplied, plot the distributions alone. With both
<code>az</code> and <code>hor</code>, show the information, azimuth, transformation and
declination panels. A single <code>index</code> is required for combined panels.
Supplying only one source input is an error, as is supplying source inputs
for an azimuth distribution. Source inputs must be named explicitly.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** An interval bar, a bearing spoke and a density curve encode different features of a measurement. Retain individual measurement identities, especially where overplotting makes repeated orientations appear to be a single observation.

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>x</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <em>skyscapeR.pdf</em> object created with either <code>az.pdf</code> or <code>coordtrans</code></p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>index</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A value to indicate which distribution to plot, when only one is desired.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>hdr</code></th><td><code>0.954</code></td><td><p>High density region to highlight. Defaults to 0.954</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Deprecated and ignored, with a warning when supplied. Provide both
<code>az</code> and <code>hor</code> for the combined panels, or omit both for distributions alone.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>xrange</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Range of x-axis to plot.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Fill colour for highest-density regions. NULL uses the current style.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>...</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Additional arguments to be passed to <em>plot</em>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Original azimuth <em>skyscapeR.pdf</em>, in the same order and with
the same number of distributions as <code>x</code>. Supply together with <code>hor</code>
to show combined panels for a single declination distribution.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>hor</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Original horizon object, or a list of horizons in the same order
and with the same length as the distributions in <code>x</code>. Supply with <code>az</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>xlim</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Earlier name for xrange.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.legend</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Show the HDR mass above stacked densities. The linked diagnostic always identifies

<code>"publication-mono"</code>. Monochrome uses grayscale and preserves line styles.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>Draws the selected probability distributions and requested intervals on the active graphics device.
</p>
```

### `plot.skyscapeR.spd()` {#fn-plot-skyscaper-spd}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-plot-skyscaper-spd)

```{=html}
<p>A peak can arise where several uncertain sightlines coincide. The horizontal axis uses
the summed curve's stored coordinate and the vertical axis its density. Optional shading
fills the area beneath the curve; changing colours or axis limits does not renormalise
it. Whether its integral is one depends on the normalisation used when creating the
object. Assess departures from a specified null using a significance test.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** An interval bar, a bearing spoke and a density curve encode different features of a measurement. Retain individual measurement identities, especially where overplotting makes repeated orientations appear to be a single observation.

### `plotAzimuth()` {#fn-plotazimuth}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-plotazimuth)

```{=html}
<p>Measurements are drawn as spokes or rim ticks. North is at the top and
bearings increase clockwise; repeated bearings can overplot. A data frame supplies the
True.Azimuth column. For optional targets the function uses the session atmosphere to compute a diurnal
track and seeks a zero-altitude crossing in the eastern and western portions of the
track. These reference bearings assume a level horizon and require the corresponding
crossings to exist.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** An interval bar, a bearing spoke and a density curve encode different features of a measurement. Retain individual measurement identities, especially where overplotting makes repeated orientations appear to be a single observation.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>az</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Azimuths in degrees clockwise from north. Can be omitted if <em>obj</em> is given.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>obj</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <em>skyscapeR.object</em> from <code>skyObject</code>, or
a list of these objects. Each group retains its own epochs and styles
for displaying the azimuths of celestial objects. Note that this assumes a single
location per group and a flat horizon of zero degrees. For a year range,
both stored declination boundaries are drawn as reference bearings.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>show.obj.labels</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Logical to control whether to display celestial objects names.
Defaults to TRUE.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>col</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Single color or color palette to use for plotting measurements.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>lty</code></th><td><code>1</code></td><td><p>Line type to plot measurements. Defaults to 1.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>lwd</code></th><td><code>1.5</code></td><td><p>Line width for measured bearings. Defaults to 1.5.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>marks</code></th><td><code>c(&quot;spokes&quot;, &quot;rim&quot;)</code></td><td><p>Draw measured orientations as equal-length <code>"spokes"</code> (default) or short <code>"rim"</code> ticks.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>obj.position</code></th><td><code>c(&quot;inside&quot;, &quot;outside&quot;)</code></td><td><p>Draw target reference lines <code>"inside"</code> the circle or just <code>"outside"</code> its rim.
```

### `plotBars()` {#fn-plotbars}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-plotbars)

```{=html}
<p>A row represents one measurement. Its horizontal bar spans the supplied value minus and
plus its uncertainty, and an optional mark shows the centre. A scalar uncertainty is
reused for all rows. Sorting rearranges measurements, labels and widths together.
Celestial overlays use the declination axis. The widths reflect the supplied
uncertainties and acquire a probability interpretation only from the measurement model.
</p>
<p>For a two-year epoch range, celestial targets are displayed as bands
covering their stored minimum and maximum declinations across the full plot
height. Single-year targets are displayed as lines.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** An interval bar, a bearing spoke and a density curve encode different features of a measurement. Retain individual measurement identities, especially where overplotting makes repeated orientations appear to be a single observation.

```{=html}
declinations. Celestial overlay values are declinations. Use them with
declination measurements, or convert measurements first using the appropriate
site and horizon. Bars show the supplied symmetric angular bounds, not fitted
confidence intervals. Use <code>az.pdf</code>, <code>coordtrans</code> and
<code>spd</code> when the full measurement distributions are needed.
</p>
```

</details>

### `spd()` {#fn-spd}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-spd)

```{=html}
<p>A summed probability density gives each input measurement one density curve. The
function linearly interpolates these curves onto one angular grid, assigns zero outside
each curve's sampled support and adds their heights point by point. With an
automatically chosen range it zeroes summed heights below the cutoff. With an explicit
range it retains the calculated heights across that range.
</p>
<p>Normalisation takes place after interpolation and any cutoff, over
the returned grid. An explicit restricted <code>xrange</code> therefore normalises
the retained portion only. Zero-area, nonfinite or negative densities and
grids with fewer than two points cannot be normalised and produce an error.
Earlier versions divided by the sum of sampled heights. Normalised outputs
now have a different scale; on a regular grid with zero endpoint densities,
new heights equal old heights divided by <code>.res</code>. Existing saved objects
are not converted. Changing resolution can still affect interpolation and
truncation accuracy, but the returned trapezoidal area is one.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Silva, F (2020) A probabilistic framework and significance test for the analysis of structural orientations
in skyscape archaeology <em>Journal of Archaeological Science</em> 118, 105138. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jas.2020.105138")}
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** A summed curve depends on its inputs, grid and normalisation. Selecting a subset changes the archaeological population being summarised. A highest-density interval describes concentrated probability mass, with no null-model adjustment.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>pdf</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>A <em>skyscapeR.pdf</em> object created with either <code>az.pdf</code> or <code>coordtrans</code></p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>xrange</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Array of values (min and max) for SPD if different from range of <em>pdf</em>. If given,
it overrides <em>.cutoff</em></p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>normalise</code></th><td><code>F</code></td><td><p>If TRUE, scale the returned density to unit area using
trapezoidal integration. Default FALSE leaves the summed density unnormalised.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.res</code></th><td><code>0.01</code></td><td><p>Resolution with which to output SPD. Default is 0.01 degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.cutoff</code></th><td><code>1e-05</code></td><td><p>When the range is chosen automatically, set summed densities below this threshold to zero. Default <code>1e-5</code>.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A <code>skyscapeR.spd</code> list with <code>metadata</code> and a <code>data</code>
data frame containing coordinate <code>x</code> (degrees) and density <code>y</code>.
Normalised densities have units of inverse degrees.
</p>
```

</details>

## Null models and significance {#group-null}

The reference distribution, score, Monte Carlo rank and any search across intervals all affect the inferential claim. A display symbol summarises an already-calculated p-value.

### `bernoulli.trial()` {#fn-bernoulli-trial}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-bernoulli-trial)

```{=html}
<p>Define a hit and the per-structure chance of a hit before counting the orientations. A
single-count probability answers how often exactly that count arises; the upper tail
answers how often a count at least that large arises.
</p>
<p>The binomial model assumes independent structures with the same
target probability <code>p</code>. The upper-tail probability is a one-sided
p-value under this model. Calculations use <code>stats::dbinom</code> and
<code>stats::pbinom</code>, avoiding factorial overflow and subtraction from 1.
At least zero hits has probability 1. With zero structures, zero hits has
probability 1 for either type. Inputs are scalar; invalid inputs error.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Ruggles, C (1999) <em>Astronomy in Prehistoric Britain and Ireland</em>. Yale University Press.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** The binomial formulation requires a defensible success probability and trial structure. Repeated structures at the same location may not act as independent trials. Delimit the target window before counting successes.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>n</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Total number of structures: a single finite nonnegative integer.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>p</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Target probability: a single finite number between 0 and 1.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>r</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Number of hits: a single finite integer between 0 and n.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>type</code></th><td><code>&quot;tail&quot;</code></td><td><p>Either <code>"single"</code> for exactly r hits or <code>"tail"</code>
for at least r hits (the default).</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A numeric probability between 0 and 1.
</p>
```

</details>

**Implementation.** `R/statistics.R`. [Full function help](help/bernoulli.trial.html) · [Null models and significance outline](contents-plan.html#plan-null)

### `modelTest()` {#fn-modeltest}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-modeltest)

```{=html}
<p>A proposed topographical or astronomical explanation can predict some orientations more
frequently than others. Testing that explanation requires simulating its predicted
distribution at the sites under study.
</p>
<p>Silva and Lomsdalen (2025) extended the random-orientation framework of Silva (2020)
to test specific hypotheses about temple orientations in Malta, including topographical and
astronomical explanations. Here the hypothesis specifies the relative probability of each
candidate orientation. A small global p-value is evidence against that particular model.
</p>
```

**Model weights and interpretation.**

```{=html}
<p>Weights are discrete sampling probabilities up to proportionality. If a
continuous model is evaluated on an uneven coordinate grid, density heights
alone do not represent probability mass; construct weights that account for
the bin widths before calling the function. Put site-specific model tables in
the same order as the observed measurements.
</p>
<p>A large p-value does not prove the proposed explanation or measure its
probability. The test asks whether the specified model is incompatible with
the observed departure statistic. Alternative models can remain compatible.
The simulations do not automatically represent dependence between sites,
selection after viewing the data, or uncertainty in fitted model parameters.
See <code>randomTest</code> for study-design and Monte Carlo limitations.
</p>



```

<details><summary>Method references</summary>

```{=html}
<p>Silva, F. (2020). A probabilistic framework and significance test for the analysis of structural orientations in skyscape archaeology. <em>Journal of Archaeological Science</em>, 118, 105138. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jas.2020.105138")}.
</p>
<p>Silva, F. and Lomsdalen, T. (2025). ‘No easy way from the earth to the stars’: a new statistical approach to the orientation of the Maltese temples. <em>Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences</em>, 17, 96. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1007/s12520-025-02208-4")}.
</p>
<p>Maris, E. and Oostenveld, R. (2007). Nonparametric statistical testing of EEG- and MEG-data. <em>Journal of Neuroscience Methods</em>. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jneumeth.2007.03.024")}.
</p>
<p>Sassenhagen, J. and Draschkow, D. (2019). Cluster-based permutation tests of MEG/EEG data do not establish significance of effect latency or location. <em>Psychophysiology</em>. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1111/psyp.13335")}.
</p>
<p>Dufour, J.-M. (2006). Monte Carlo tests with nuisance parameters: A general approach to finite-sample inference and nonstandard asymptotics. <em>Journal of Econometrics</em>, 133, 443-477. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jeconom.2005.06.007")}.
</p>
<p>North, B. V., Curtis, D. and Sham, P. C. (2002). A note on the calculation of empirical P values from Monte Carlo procedures. <em>American Journal of Human Genetics</em>, 71, 439-441. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1086/341527")}.
</p>



```

</details>

**Interpretation and limits.** Preserve the generating model, measurement-to-site mapping, simulation seed, comparison grid and rank convention. A change in the null answers a different archaeological question even when the same observed curve is used.


<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>pdf</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Empirical skyscapeR.pdf from <code>az.pdf</code>, <code>dec.pdf</code> or <code>coordtrans</code>. Its coordinate selects the simulation path.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>model</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>One shared data frame or an ordered list with one table per observation. The first column contains candidate coordinates in degrees and the second contains nonnegative discrete sampling weights, with at least one positive weight. On equally spaced grids, density heights can serve as weights.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>unc</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Positive standard deviation (normal) or half-width (uniform), in degrees of the tested coordinate. Supply a scalar or one per observation. Omit to reuse stored measurement uncertainties or mean-shift transformed declination curves. See Details.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>nsims</code></th><td><code>1000</code></td><td><p>Number of simulations, at least two. Default is 1000.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>conf</code></th><td><code>0.95</code></td><td><p>Confidence level as a fraction.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>tails</code></th><td><code>2</code></td><td><p>1 for upper excesses, 2 for excesses and deficits.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>normalise</code></th><td><code>FALSE</code></td><td><p>Scale each summed density to unit area before comparison.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>.res</code></th><td><code>0.01</code></td><td><p>Spacing of the empirical and simulated comparison grids in degrees. Default 0.01.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>ncores</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Worker count. By default use half the detected available logical cores, rounded down with a minimum of one. Set ncores=1 for serial execution. The simulation count and memory batch size can further limit workers. Verbose output reports the effective count.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>verbose</code></th><td><code>TRUE</code></td><td><p>Display simulation progress.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><p>A dash means the signature supplies no default expression. The function may resolve an omitted value internally.</p><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.sigTest list with settings and global/local results in metadata, empirical density and null envelope in data.
</p><h5>Model weights and interpretation</h5><p>Weights are discrete sampling probabilities up to proportionality. If a
continuous model is evaluated on an uneven coordinate grid, density heights

the same order as the observed measurements.
</p><p>A large p-value does not prove the proposed explanation or measure its
probability. The test asks whether the specified model is incompatible with
the observed departure statistic. Alternative models can remain compatible.
The simulations do not automatically represent dependence between sites,
selection after viewing the data, or uncertainty in fitted model parameters.
See <code>randomTest</code> for study-design and Monte Carlo limitations.
</p>
```

### `plot.skyscapeR.sigTest()` {#fn-plot-skyscaper-sigtest}

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-plot-skyscaper-sigtest)

```{=html}
<p>The observed curve and envelope use the azimuth or declination grid stored in the test
result. The two-tailed display shades between its lower and upper pointwise bounds; the
one-tailed display shades up to the upper bound from zero. Optional annotations show the
stored global p-value and the local intervals, coloured by deficit or excess and
labelled by p-value symbols. The observed and envelope curves jointly set the visible vertical range. The lower panel identifies adjusted and legacy unadjusted local results. The plot reads the fitted result without repeating the
simulations. New local values use maximum-cluster adjustment under the complete null;
cluster endpoints remain descriptive, not confidence limits. Legacy fits retain their
original unadjusted values. Interpret local regions alongside the whole-curve test.
</p>
```

**Interpretation and limits.** Keep the numerical global and adjusted local p-values with the output. Symbol thresholds and the placement of a band on the plot do not supply extra precision about its endpoints.
